t: At the Very Bottom, You Can Hear God Send You Again
v: Then Jonah prayed to the LORD, his God, out of the fish’s belly.
He said, “I called because of my affliction to the LORD. He answered me. Out of the belly of Sheol I cried. You heard my voice.
“When my soul fainted within me, I remembered the LORD. My prayer came in to you, into your holy temple.
Those who regard vain idols forsake their own mercy.
But I will sacrifice to you with the voice of thanksgiving. I will pay that which I have vowed. Salvation belongs to the LORD.”
Then the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited out Jonah on the dry land.
The LORD’s word came to Jonah the second time, saying,
“Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and preach to it the message that I give you.”
So Jonah arose, and went to Nineveh, according to the LORD’s word. Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city, three days’ journey across.
Jonah began to enter into the city a day’s journey, and he cried out, and said, “In forty days, Nineveh will be overthrown!”
The people of Nineveh believed God; and they proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from their greatest even to their least.
b: In the belly of the fish, Jonah came to the darkest and most helpless moment of his life. He had no strength left to run and no excuse left to give; all he could do was cry out to God. Remarkably, when he called from “the depths of Sheol,” God had not gone far away. He bent down and listened. This shows us an important truth: when a person reaches the end of himself and is willing to turn back to God, that very place becomes the starting point of a new meeting. It is not that circumstances changed God; it is that the person finally let go of himself and turned to the Lord.

When Jonah’s heart fainted within him, he “remembered the Lord,” and he declared one pivotal sentence: “Salvation belongs to the Lord.” This was not a slogan but a complete reversal in how he saw things. He no longer relied on his own judgment or let his feelings rule. He acknowledged that rescue, sovereignty and every decision are in God’s hands. This is the beginning of selflessness and the decisive moment of letting Jesus be King. When a person lets go of self, God’s work begins to unfold.

Then we see that God’s grace does not stop at rescue; it moves on to sending. The word of the Lord came to Jonah “the second time.” God did not bring up the past, and he did not cancel the calling. He simply said again, “Arise!” This is the voice of restoration. This time Jonah obeyed, and the whole city of Nineveh repented, from the king to the people, humbling themselves before God. It reminds us that a person restored by grace often becomes the channel through which other lives are turned around.
a: Turn to God in the low place
When you feel you cannot go on, do not run away. Crying out to God is a new beginning.
Acknowledge that sovereignty is in God’s hands
Learn to let go of your own ideas and declare, “Salvation belongs to the Lord,” letting Jesus be King.
Obey God’s second calling
Do not let past failures define you. God still wants to use you to bless others.
q: Am I willing, even at my lowest point, to turn back to God and answer the calling he is giving me again?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, when I am lost like Jonah, running away and falling into the depths, thank You for still hearing my cry. Help me let go of myself and acknowledge Your sovereignty, and let Jesus be King in my life. Give me courage to answer Your sending once more, so that my life may become a vessel of blessing to others. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I turn to God in my lowest place. Salvation belongs to the Lord, and I will be sent again.

t: When Surrounded on Every Side, Place Your Whole Life in God’s Hands
v: For I have heard the slander of many, terror on every side, while they conspire together against me, they plot to take away my life.
But I trust in you, LORD. I said, “You are my God.”
My times are in your hand. Deliver me from the hand of my enemies, and from those who persecute me.
Make your face to shine on your servant. Save me in your loving kindness.
Let me not be disappointed, LORD, for I have called on you. Let the wicked be disappointed. Let them be silent in Sheol.
Let the lying lips be mute, which speak against the righteous insolently, with pride and contempt.
b: David does not hide his real situation: outside are slander, scheming and terror; inside are the fear of being pressed and attacked. This is not weakness but an honest picture of life. People who belong to God do not escape malice and misunderstanding; rather, under pressure they choose to bring their real pain to God instead of holding themselves up on their own. Faith is not denying the storm; it is turning to God in the middle of it.

In such a situation David makes a pivotal declaration: “But I trust in you. I said, ‘You are my God.’” This is not a confession made after his mood improved; it is a choice of faith made while the danger was still present. Then he says, “My times are in your hand.” This is an attitude of complete entrusting: no longer gripping control, no longer rushing to defend himself, but letting God be King. This is selflessness in practice, and trust that flows from the heart.

David did not reach out to take revenge, nor did he fight lies with lies. He handed justice over to God. He knew that what makes a person stand firm is not a human effort to clear his name but the light of God’s face and his loving kindness. When a person is willing to place shame, attacks and the future into God’s hands, God becomes his covering; he silences the lies and gives the righteous rest.
a: Choose to trust God when misunderstood
When you cannot clear your name and are surrounded, go to God first instead of rushing to prove yourself to people.
Return the lordship of your life to the Lord
Each day practice saying sincerely, “My times are in your hand,” and let Jesus be King.
Replace revenge with trust
Do not answer attacks with temper. Entrust justice to God and let his loving kindness be your covering.
q: In the situation that presses on me and wounds me most right now, have I truly placed the sovereignty in God’s hands?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, when I am misunderstood, attacked and full of fear, thank You that You are still my God. Today I am willing to place my whole life in Your hands, not arguing on my own and not responding in anger. Make Your face shine on me and save me by Your loving kindness, so that in You I may have peace and strength to stand firm. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: My times are in God’s hand. I trust in the Lord, and I will not be put to shame.

t: When People Scatter, God Still Provides Companions for the Road
v: Be diligent to come to me soon,
for Demas left me, having loved this present world, and went to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia; and Titus to Dalmatia.
Only Luke is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service.
But I sent Tychicus to Ephesus.
Bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus when you come—and the books, especially the parchments.
b: This passage shows us Paul, old, imprisoned and near martyrdom, openly revealing his loneliness and need. He did not pretend to be strong, and he did not cover reality with spiritual language. He honestly said, “Be diligent to come to me soon.” Following Jesus does not mean we do not need people. Spiritual maturity is not refusing companionship; it is knowing how to open up to the right people at the right time.

Paul writes, “Demas left me, having loved this present world.” This is not criticism but a reminder: not everyone who once walked with you will walk with you to the end. Some turn away because the world draws them; others are sent in different directions by different missions. This does not mean Paul failed; it shows that people coming and going is part of the road of service. What matters is not whether people stay, but whether we remain faithful in the place God has given us.

In what looked like loneliness, God still kept Luke with Paul and even restored the broken relationship with Mark. Mark, who had once disappointed Paul, was now “useful to me for service.” We see that God is the one who mends relationships and renews vessels. Finally, Paul mentions his cloak and his books, especially the parchments, showing that to the very end of his life he still hungered for God’s word and still valued learning and reflection. Even in cold, loneliness and prison, he chose to let Jesus be King and to run the last stretch with all his heart.
a: When people leave, entrust rather than turn bitter
Not everyone who walks with you will go all the way. Give the loss to God and do not let your heart harden.
Treasure those whom God leaves beside you
Do not look only at Demas who left; thank God also for Luke who remains.
Hold on to your connection with the Lord in loneliness
Whatever the circumstances, keep drawing near to God’s word and let your life be renewed again and again.
q: When I experience the loss of relationships or disappointment, do I still choose to trust God’s arrangement?
pr: Lord Jesus, when I feel lonely, left behind, or hurt in my relationships, heal my heart so that I do not become bitter or draw back. Thank You that You know my real needs and prepare companions for my road. Help me, in any circumstance, to keep hungering for Your word and to finish faithfully the course You have entrusted to me. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Though people come and go, the Lord walks with me, and I will faithfully finish the course God has given me.

t: Not Holding On by Yourself, but Standing in the Lord
v: Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might.
Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.

For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world’s rulers of the darkness of this age, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.
Therefore put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.
Stand therefore, having the utility belt of truth buckled around your waist, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness,
and having fitted your feet with the preparation of the Good News of peace,
above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the fiery darts of the evil one.
And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God;
with all prayer and requests, praying at all times in the Spirit, and being watchful to this end in all perseverance and requests for all the saints.
Pray for me, that utterance may be given to me in opening my mouth, to make known with boldness the mystery of the Good News,
for which I am an ambassador in chains; that in it I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak.
b: At the close of his letter, Paul reminds believers of something vital: true strength does not come from ourselves but is found “in the Lord, and in the strength of his might.” We often think maturity means being able to endure, to last long, to carry much. But the spiritual truth is that the more we rely on ourselves, the easier we are knocked down; the more selfless we become and the more we lean on Jesus, the more firmly we stand. Letting Jesus be King is not bravado; it is admitting, “I need him.”

Paul then points out that our real battle is not against people, circumstances or emotions, but against unseen spiritual powers. This reminds us that much of our inner weariness, confusion, accusation and fear is not merely psychological but spiritual warfare. Answering a spiritual problem with human methods only brings more chaos. Only by putting on the armor God provides, and standing in truth, righteousness, salvation and faith, can we avoid being led around by the enemy’s schemes.

Finally, Paul brings the focus back to “praying at all times in the Spirit.” The key to the armor working is not technique but relationship with God. Armor without prayer is only a shell; without God’s word the sword loses its edge. True victory is not how many enemies we defeat but that in the evil day we are still able “to stand.” This is a posture of life: relying on the Holy Spirit with the heart, not on ourselves with the mind.
a: Stop holding on by your own strength
When you are weary, come back to the Lord first instead of pushing yourself to do a little more.
Meet spiritual battles in a spiritual way
When confusion, accusation and fear come, pray and return to the truth first instead of rushing to strike back at people.
Build a steady life of prayer and Bible reading
Put on the spiritual armor every day, making God’s word and the Holy Spirit’s guidance the normal rhythm of life.
q: Is the struggle I face now actually calling me back to relying on the Lord rather than on myself?
pr: Lord Jesus, I admit that I often try to solve problems on my own and only grow more tired. Today I choose to come back to You, admit my limits and receive Your power. Teach me to put on the armor You have given, to stand in truth, to move forward in faith and to walk with You in prayer, so that I am not shaken in any battle. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I do not hold on by my own strength; I stand firm in the great power of the Lord.

t: Stop Putting It Off. Start Preparing Today
v: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise;
which having no chief, overseer, or ruler,
provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest.
How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you arise out of your sleep?
A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep—
so your poverty will come as a robber, and your scarcity as an armed man.
b: God speaks to us through the tiny ant, showing that wisdom is not a matter of rank but of the attitude of life. No one commands the ant and no system restrains her, yet she knows “what to do now.” She does not wait for a feeling or an order; she prepares in season. This reminds us that a mature life is not one that moves only when pushed, but one that acts on its own out of reverence for God, letting his word be the standard.

In this passage, laziness is not only about doing no work; it is an attitude of delay, numbness and “later.” “A little more sleep” seems harmless, yet it steals the strength of life little by little. The enemy’s most common tool is not great sin but keeping people postponing obedience, postponing repentance, postponing action, until want arrives suddenly and there is no time left to prepare.

From a spiritual point of view, the wisdom of the ant reminds us to respond to God while there is still light, time and prompting. If we do not prepare today, tomorrow we may lack the strength to stand. A selfless life is not passive; it lets Jesus be King and is willing to be led by the Holy Spirit, acting at the moment action is needed.
a: Respond to God’s reminder today
Do not leave the Holy Spirit’s prompting for later. Take one small step of obedience today.
Build steady, lasting good habits
Like the ant, a little each day will build up strength in your life.
Store up spiritual provision for the future
Reading the Bible, praying and practicing the life daily are preparation for the challenges ahead.
q: Is there a “wait a bit longer” in my life that is quietly stealing the blessing God wants to give me?
pr: Lord, shine Your light on the places in my life where I am lazy and putting things off. Do not let me miss the time to obey, nor lose the preparation I should have because I delayed. Give me a faithful and watchful heart like the ant’s, so that each day I walk according to Your word. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will not delay any longer. Today I respond to God’s leading.

t: Peace Comes Not From a High City but From Trusting God
v: In that day, this song will be sung in the land of Judah: “We have a strong city. God appoints salvation for walls and bulwarks.
Open the gates, that the righteous nation may enter: the one which keeps faith.
You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.
Trust in the LORD forever; for in the LORD, the LORD, is an everlasting Rock.
For he has brought down those who dwell on high, the lofty city. He lays it low. He lays it low even to the ground. He brings it even to the dust.
b: This passage paints a sharp contrast: on one side, the strong city that God builds; on the other, the lofty city that people consider secure. True safety does not come from outward defenses, status or resources, but from the Lord himself becoming the wall. When God’s salvation is the wall, the city is not held up by human strength but by God’s faithfulness.

The gates God opens admit only “the righteous nation that keeps faith.” This does not mean flawless people, but those whose hearts are toward God, who trust him and do not rely on themselves. Righteousness here is not self-righteousness but reliance on God’s righteousness; faith is not a slogan but a choice of life. When a person is willing to be selfless, handing the sovereignty to Jesus and letting him be King, he walks into the safe place God has prepared.

The heart of the passage is one deep promise: “You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace.” Peace does not mean there are no storms; it means the heart is held steady by God. This peace comes from single-minded trust, not half-belief, but placing the whole heart on God. The lofty cities people boast of will eventually fall; only the Lord is the everlasting Rock, unchanging forever.
a: Put your security back in God
Do not use money, ability or plans as your walls. Learn to let God’s salvation be your true protection.
Practice a single-minded trust
When your heart begins to panic, deliberately turn your thoughts to God’s word and meet anxiety with faith.
Choose to stand on the Rock in turmoil
Circumstances may shake, but if each day you obey the Holy Spirit and do God’s word, you will stand firm.
q: Is my sense of security built on God, the Rock, or on the “high city” I have built for myself?
pr: Lord, thank You for being my Rock and my wall. When I easily rely on myself and on circumstances, draw my heart back so that I trust in You alone. Let my heart find true peace in You, unshaken by turmoil around me. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I trust steadfastly in the Lord. My peace is in him and will never be shaken.

t: What God Begins, He Will Surely Finish
v: I thank my God whenever I remember you,
always in every request of mine on behalf of you all, making my requests with joy,
for your partnership in furtherance of the Good News from the first day until now;
being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.

It is even right for me to think this way on behalf of all of you, because I have you in my heart, because both in my bonds and in the defense and confirmation of the Good News, you all are partakers with me of grace.
For God is my witness, how I long after all of you in the tender mercies of Christ Jesus.
This I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and all discernment,
so that you may approve the things that are excellent, that you may be sincere and without offense to the day of Christ,
being filled with the fruits of righteousness which are through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.
b: Whenever Paul thought of the brothers and sisters in Philippi, his heart filled with thanks and joy. It was not because they were perfect, but because “from the first day until now” they had stood with the gospel. True co-workers do not merely work together; they live for the same focus, that Jesus would receive the glory.

The most precious line in the passage is this: “He who began a good work in you will complete it.” The starting point of faith is not human determination but God’s doing, and its end is not our holding on but God’s faithfulness. Many people have no confidence in themselves, but God has never lost confidence in his own work. Whatever God begins, he will see through to the end.

Paul did not stand above people making demands; he stood in love, praying for them. He hoped their love would not stay in feeling but grow in truth, mature in discernment, and bear the fruit of righteousness in daily life. Maturity of life is not outward performance but being shaped within by Christ, so that God receives the glory.
a: Believe God is at work in your life
Even if you feel weak and progress is slow, do not write yourself off, because God is not finished.
Focus on life, not only on ministry
More important than how much you do is whether you bear the fruit of life, so that people see Christ.
Walk together in prayer and love
Learn from Paul to long for people with the heart of Christ and to accompany them on the heavenly road with prayer.
q: Do I truly believe that the work God began, he will also complete in me?
pr: Lord, thank You for the good work You have begun in my life. When I am discouraged, doubtful or want to give up, remind me that it is not I who hold on but You who bring it to completion. Let me bear fruit all my life that brings You glory, until the day I see Your face. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: The good work God has begun in me, he will personally complete until the day of Christ.

t: In the Kingdom of Heaven, the Smaller You Are, the Greater
v: In that hour the disciples came to Jesus, saying, “Who then is greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven?”
Jesus called a little child to himself, and set him in the middle of them
and said, “Most certainly I tell you, unless you turn and become as little children, you will in no way enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.
Whoever therefore humbles himself as this little child is the greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven.
b: The disciples asked a very “human” question: who is greater? Who is more important? Who has the higher position? The question reveals a deep desire in the human heart to be seen, affirmed and lifted up. Yet Jesus did not answer with theory. He called a little child and turned the standard of the Kingdom completely upside down.

Jesus said that unless we “turn” and become like little children, we cannot even enter the Kingdom. This does not mean becoming childish; it means returning to a simple, dependent life without craving power. A child does not fight for position, does not know comparison and does not grasp for authority; he only trusts, depends and receives. This is the entrance to the life of the Kingdom.

In the Kingdom, the greatest is not the most capable but the one most willing to let go of himself. Humility is not thinking little of yourself; it is putting yourself back in the right place: letting people be people and God be God. When a person no longer exalts himself, is willing to be selfless and lets Jesus be King, God lifts him up instead. This is not a promotion made by people but the natural order of God’s Kingdom.
a: Let go of comparison
Stop asking, “Am I greater than so-and-so?” and ask instead, “Am I becoming more like Jesus?” Comparison only brings pride or inferiority; simplicity brings freedom.
Practice turning like a child
Each day admit your limits before God. Do not rely on analysis or grasp for control; trust the Holy Spirit’s guidance with your heart.
Choose humility in relationships
Do not grab for position or fight over who is right. Be willing to step back and let love go first, so that the life of Christ is seen.
q: In my heart, am I still chasing “who is greater,” or am I now willing to follow Jesus simply?
pr: Lord Jesus, thank You for teaching me the truth of the Kingdom through a little child. Lead me to turn, to stop living in comparison and pride, and give me a simple, humble heart that is willing to depend on You. Let me not exalt myself but exalt You alone, and let You reign as King in my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am willing to be humble like a little child and simply follow Jesus in the order of the Kingdom of Heaven.

t: It Looks Small Now, but God Says, “Greater Glory Is Coming”
v: In the seventh month, in the twenty-first day of the month, the LORD’s word came by Haggai the prophet, saying,
“Speak now to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to the remnant of the people, saying,
‘Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How do you see it now? Isn’t it in your eyes as nothing?

Yet now be strong, Zerubbabel,’ says the LORD. ‘Be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. Be strong, all you people of the land,’ says the LORD, ‘and work, for I am with you,’ says the LORD of Armies.
This is the word that I covenanted with you when you came out of Egypt, and my Spirit lived among you. ‘Don’t be afraid.’
For this is what the LORD of Armies says: ‘Yet once more, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land;
and I will shake all nations. The treasure of all nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of Armies.
The silver is mine, and the gold is mine,’ says the LORD of Armies.
‘The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former,’ says the LORD of Armies; ‘and in this place I will give peace,’ says the LORD of Armies.”
b: God did not deny the gap the people saw. The returned exiles looked with their own eyes at the new temple, and compared with the glory of Solomon’s day it truly seemed “as nothing.” Yet God did not scold their sense of loss. He said to them directly, “Be strong and work, for I am with you.” What God values is not the size of what is before us, but whether, when things look small, we still choose to obey, keep going and stay faithful.

God reminded them that the key is not resources or outward glory but “my Spirit lived among you.” When the people came out of Egypt they had nothing, yet because of God’s presence they became a turning point in history. In the same way, this building was not driven by gold and silver but by God’s presence. When people do not shrink back because of circumstances and are willing to go on working selflessly, God himself takes charge of the glory that results.

Finally God declared a promise beyond human sight: “The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former.” This does not refer only to a building but to the work of God’s Kingdom. True glory is not the splendor people see but the peace that God’s presence brings. When Jesus came to the temple, and God himself dwelt among people, this promise was fully fulfilled. God’s glory is always deeper, truer and more lasting than the past people remember with longing.
a: Do not lose heart because it “looks small”
Your service, family or life-work may not be dazzling now, but God is working in it. Do not use past glory to dismiss today’s obedience.
Hold on to presence, not conditions
Learn to shift your focus from “what do I have?” to “is God with me?” With the Lord present, small becomes great.
Keep working and let God take care of the glory
You only need to be faithful, strong and obedient. Leave the glory and the results to God to complete.
q: Do I doubt that God is working in my life just because things are not as I expected?
pr: Lord, You know the sense of loss in my heart over what is “not as it was.” Help me not to look at circumstances or size but to fix my eyes on Your presence. Give me a strong heart to keep obeying in what seems small, and to believe that You are preparing greater glory and true peace. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Even though it looks small now, I believe God will bring greater glory and peace.

t: Money Can Be Used for Living, but It Cannot Be Relied On
v: But godliness with contentment is great gain.
For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out.
But having food and clothing, we will be content with that.
But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction.
For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
But you, man of God, flee these things, and follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness.
Fight the good fight of faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called, and you confessed the good confession in the sight of many witnesses.
Charge those who are rich in this present age that they not be arrogant, nor have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy;
that they do good, that they be rich in good works, that they be ready to distribute, willing to share;
laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold of eternal life.
b: Paul does not condemn money itself. He points directly at a core question of life: what does a person truly rely on? Money can be used, but it cannot carry the weight of a life. If we place our security, worth and future on wealth, we are unconsciously pulled along by it and may even drift from the faith. The real “great gain” is not having more but godliness together with contentment, with the heart held steady by God.

Paul reminds us that we came into the world with nothing and will leave with nothing. If the heart is not content, even great wealth will be driven by desire and fall into anxiety, comparison and sorrow. Love of money is dangerous not because there is too much money, but because hope has been put in the wrong place and money has taken the place of God.

So Paul gives a clear direction to the man of God: not to pursue more, but to pursue a better quality of life. Righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience and gentleness cannot be bought in the market, yet they are the marks of eternal life. To the rich, Paul does not say to feel guilty, but to shift their focus: not to rely on uncertain riches but on the God who richly provides everything, and to turn resources into blessing, laying a foundation for eternity.
a: Re-examine what I rely on
Ask yourself: when I am anxious, do I want to grasp money more, or God more?
Practice contentment and let the heart rest
Each day give thanks for what God has already supplied, rather than staring at what you do not yet have.
Let resources be a blessing, not a shackle
Use what God gave you for doing good, sharing and loving others, storing up true treasure for eternity.
q: Does my deepest sense of security come from money or from God?
pr: Heavenly Father, shine Your light on my heart so that I am not pulled along by uncertain riches but rely on You alone. Teach me contentment in everything, and let You be my true safety and joy. Help me also to use rightly what You have given me, so that my life lays a foundation for eternity. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I do not rely on riches; I rely only on the God who richly gives us all things, and I take hold of the life that is truly life.

t: Not Trying Harder, but Learning to Rest
v: Let’s fear therefore, lest perhaps anyone of you should seem to have come short of a promise of entering into his rest.
For indeed we have had good news preached to us, even as they also did, but the word they heard didn’t profit them, because it wasn’t mixed with faith by those who heard.
For we who have believed do enter into that rest, even as he has said, “As I swore in my wrath, they will not enter into my rest;” although the works were finished from the foundation of the world.
For he has said this somewhere about the seventh day, “God rested on the seventh day from all his works;”
Seeing therefore it remains that some should enter into it, and they to whom the good news was preached before failed to enter in because of disobedience,
For if Joshua had given them rest, he would not have spoken afterward of another day.
There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God.
For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his.
Let’s therefore give diligence to enter into that rest, lest anyone fall after the same example of disobedience.
b: This passage reminds us of a deep but often overlooked truth: people lose rest not because they do not try hard enough, but because they do not believe enough. The Israelites did hear the good news and God’s promise, but the problem was that the word “wasn’t mixed with faith by those who heard.” The word entered the ears but not the heart; they heard, but did not entrust themselves, and so they lived in toil, fear and unrest.

God’s rest is not something only for the future; it was prepared from the foundation of the world. On the seventh day God rested, not because he was tired, but to declare that “all is finished.” A life that has entered rest no longer proves its worth by performance or maintains its security by effort, but believes that God has already completed what he needed to complete. Unbelievers strain at work; believers learn to rest.

The writer points out that true rest was not fully realized when Joshua led the people into Canaan; it remains a spiritual state kept for God’s people. The key to this rest is not stopping all action, but “resting from his works”: no longer centered on self, no longer being our own king, but letting Jesus be King and the Holy Spirit guide. This is the selfless life that 321 emphasizes: not I holding up my life, but Christ living in me.
a: Examine whether I am working hard to prove myself
If I am constantly tired, anxious and unable to stop, perhaps it is not that there is too much to do, but that my heart has not truly trusted God.
Practice answering God’s word with faith
Do not only hear and know, but choose to believe and obey, leaving the results to God.
Deliberately enter spiritual rest each day
Through prayer, stillness and entrusting, remind yourself: God has finished it, and I do not need to be my own king.
q: Is my busyness now an obedience of faith, or an anxious effort to hold myself up?
pr: Heavenly Father, I admit that I often work in my own way and forget to rest in faith. Forgive me for the toil that unbelief brings. Today I choose to believe Your word and rest from my own works, letting Jesus be King in my life and the Holy Spirit lead my every step. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I no longer hold up my life by myself; by faith I enter the rest God has prepared.

t: When Things Are Stuck, Stop Pushing on Your Own
v: The angel who talked with me came again and wakened me, as a man who is wakened out of his sleep.

He said to me, “What do you see?” I said, “I have seen, and behold, a lamp stand all of gold, with its bowl on the top of it, and its seven lamps on it; there are seven pipes to each of the lamps which are on the top of it;
and two olive trees by it, one on the right side of the bowl, and the other on the left side of it.”
I answered and spoke to the angel who talked with me, saying, “What are these, my lord?”
Then the angel who talked with me answered me, “Don’t you know what these are?” I said, “No, my lord.”
Then he answered and spoke to me, saying, “This is the LORD’s word to Zerubbabel, saying, ‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says the LORD of Armies.
Who are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you are a plain; and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of ‘Grace, grace, to it!’”
Moreover the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
“The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house. His hands shall also finish it; and you will know that the LORD of Armies has sent me to you.

Indeed, who despises the day of small things? For these seven shall rejoice, and shall see the plumb line in the hand of Zerubbabel. These are the LORD’s eyes, which run back and forth through the whole earth.”
b: Zechariah was awakened by the angel, as if called back to reality from a spiritual slumber. The vision before him was a lampstand, not lit by people but supplied with oil continually by two olive trees, picturing that the light of life is not maintained by human effort but comes from God and is supplied without stopping. The people had been rebuilding the temple for years under hindrance, with hard circumstances and discouraged hearts, yet God first let them see one thing: the true source of the work is not human ability but God’s supply.

God spoke the key words to Zerubbabel: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.” This does not deny effort; it points to the root. Might stands for outward resources and power for personal ability, but a work of God resting on those two alone will eventually get stuck. What truly moves God’s Kingdom forward is the Holy Spirit’s guidance and power. When a person is willing to be selfless, to stop being his own king and let the Holy Spirit lead, what looked like a great mountain of difficulty becomes a plain before God.

God also warned the people not to despise “the day of small things.” In discouragement we most easily look down on small progress before us, thinking it is not worth it or not important. But God’s eyes run through the whole earth, and he rejoiced when he saw the plumb line in Zerubbabel’s hand. God values not size but whether we obey his guidance, not speed but whether we walk in his will. If God is the beginning, he himself will be the completion.
a: Stop and check whom I am relying on
When things will not move, ask yourself: am I relying on my own ability, or waiting for the Holy Spirit’s guidance?
Do not despise today’s small progress
Be faithful in the small things God has entrusted to you now, and believe God is working in them.
Hand the sovereignty over “getting it done” to God
I take care of obeying and following; the results I leave to God, letting Jesus be King.
q: On the thing I most want to break through now, am I holding on by myself, or willing to hand it to the Holy Spirit to lead?
pr: Heavenly Father, I admit that I often want to do things my own way and neglect to rely on You. Today I am willing to let go of my pride in might and ability and place my life and service in Your hands. Holy Spirit, lead me and fill me, so that in You I may accomplish what You want completed. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am not getting through by holding on by myself. I rely on the Holy Spirit, and God’s work will be completed.

t: See the Likeness of Christ in One Another
v: If therefore there is any exhortation in Christ, if any consolation of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any tender mercies and compassion,
make my joy full by being like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind;
doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
Do all things without complaining and arguing,
that you may become blameless and harmless, children of God without defect in the middle of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you are seen as lights in the world,
holding up the word of life, that I may have something to boast in the day of Christ that I didn’t run in vain nor labor in vain.
Yes, and if I am poured out on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with you all.
In the same way, you also should be glad and rejoice with me.
But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that I also may be cheered up when I know how you are doing.
For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you.
b: Paul begins not with commands but with the foundation “in Christ.” True unity is not sameness of personality or similarity of background; it is that we share one life in Christ. The love of the same Lord and the fellowship of the same Spirit give people who were different one direction. This kind of unity is not outward cooperation but an alignment of the life within, with Jesus as the common focus.

Paul then identifies the most deadly roots that break relationships: rivalry, empty glory, and unwillingness to let go of self. When a person wants to prove himself, protect himself and fight for his place, it is hard to truly see others. But humility is not putting yourself down; it is handing sovereignty back to God, willingly returning to your place as a human being, and letting Jesus be King. When a person is selfless, he naturally cares for others, and relationships are built up.

Paul goes on to remind us that a life belonging to God will be seen in daily life, especially in the most real moments: “without murmurings and disputes.” In a crooked and perverse generation, grumbling comes naturally and arguing seems reasonable, but God’s children are called to live a different brightness. This kind of life is not propped up by effort; it comes from the life of Christ within, willing to pay a price for others. Paul was glad to be poured out, and Timothy genuinely cared for the church, both because Christ lived in them.
a: Make Christ the center of relationships
In every relationship do not ask who is right or wrong; first ask how Jesus wants to be King here.
Practice selflessness rather than fighting to win
In conflict choose humility and yielding, letting life win over argument.
Shine differently in daily life
Start with no grumbling and no disputing, so that people see the life of Christ through you.
q: In my most recent relationship, am I holding on to myself, or letting the mind of Christ rule?
pr: Lord Jesus, thank You for first letting go of Yourself for me and becoming my example. Put Your mind and thoughts in me, so that I do not strive for myself but live out Your life. Holy Spirit, lead me to learn humility and love in every relationship, so that people see You through me. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I do not live for myself; I let the life of Christ shine in me.

t: Close Your Fist and the Blessing Cannot Flow
v: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which the LORD your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother;
but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks.

Beware that there not be a wicked thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand,” and your eye be evil against your poor brother and you give him nothing; and he cry to the LORD against you, and it be sin to you.
You shall surely give, and your heart shall not be grieved when you give to him, because it is for this thing the LORD your God will bless you in all your work and in all that you put your hand to.
For the poor will never cease out of the land. Therefore I command you to surely open your hand to your brother, to your needy, and to your poor, in your land.
b: This passage does not begin with a system but deals first with the human “heart.” God knows that people harden most easily in calculation, especially when giving may affect their own security, and then they begin to harden the heart, clench the hand and look for reasons. God makes it clear that the real problem is not whether the hand has anything, but whether the heart is willing to trust him. A heart that will not open is often afraid of the future rather than believing in God’s provision.

God goes further in exposing a spiritual danger: when people wrap selfishness in spiritual reasons, sin slips in quietly. The year of release was meant to be grace, yet it could be used as an excuse not to give. This reminds us that faith reduced to calculation and self-protection has already left God’s heart. What God values is not how much we give but whether we give with faith and love, rather than with grief and reluctance.

Finally, God gives a heavenly logic: open your hand, and blessing comes on all you do. This is not an exchange of conditions but the natural flow of a life that belongs to God. God’s people are not the end point of resources but channels of blessing. When a person is willing to be selfless and let God be King, entrusting his security to the Lord, life is no longer bound by the fear of “not enough” but enters freedom and abundance.
a: Examine your “clenched-fist moments”
Think about the times you have shut the door of your heart to someone in need because you worried about the future.
Practice generosity by faith
When you give, you are not only giving away; you are declaring, my supply is in God’s hands.
Let blessing flow rather than be hoarded
Ask yourself: is there room for what God has given me to flow to others?
q: The last time I did not want to give, did not dare to give, or was unwilling to give, what was I really afraid of?
pr: Heavenly Father, shine Your light on my heart and let me see the places where I clench from fear. Help me believe that You are my provider, not I myself. Give me a soft, generous, unreckoning heart, so that when I give it is not with grief but with joy. Make my life a vessel through which blessing flows. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I open my hand and trust God, and blessing will flow in my life.

t: Where You Run Decides Whether You Stand Firm
v: A man who isolates himself pursues selfishness, and defies all sound judgment.
A fool has no delight in understanding, but only in revealing his own opinion.
When wickedness comes, contempt also comes, and with shame comes disgrace.
The words of a man’s mouth are like deep waters. The fountain of wisdom is like a flowing brook.
To be partial to the faces of the wicked is not good, nor to deprive the innocent of justice.
A fool’s lips come into strife, and his mouth invites beatings.
A fool’s mouth is his destruction, and his lips are a snare to his soul.
The words of a gossip are like dainty morsels: they go down into a person’s innermost parts.
One who is slack in his work is brother to him who is a master of destruction.
The LORD’s name is a strong tower: the righteous run to him, and are safe.
The rich man’s wealth is his strong city, like an unscalable wall in his own imagination.
Before destruction the heart of man is proud, but before honor is humility.
b: This passage is like a spiritual mirror that shows the true condition of the human heart. A person who only wants to satisfy and display himself will refuse wisdom and refuse the reminders of others. Such a person seems to have strong opinions, but in fact shuts himself into isolation and folly. His words turn into deep, murky water, bringing not life but strife and ruin.

The passage keeps reminding us that the mouth and the heart are connected. A proud heart speaks words that stir up trouble; a slack life heads toward waste and emptiness. If a person puts his security in possessions, ability or his own judgment, his heart builds a “seemingly secure” high wall, but that wall exists only in imagination, and when a shaking comes it falls more easily.

The real contrast is made in verse 10: the name of the Lord is the strong tower. The righteous do not stand by themselves; they choose to run to God. Running to him means admitting our limits; running to him means putting down pride; running to him means letting Jesus be King. Honor does not come from lifting ourselves up but begins with humility and trusting God. This is the path of a life that belongs to God.
a: Examine my true source of security
When I am afraid, uneasy or frustrated, whom do I run to first: God, or my own methods and resources?
Practice letting wisdom into relationships
Do not only want to say your own thoughts; be willing to listen and to be reminded, and let God’s true wisdom correct me.
Choose humility rather than self-exaltation
Each day deliberately hand the sovereignty to Jesus, not proving yourself with words but witnessing to him with your life.
q: When I feel uneasy, what is the “strong city” my heart most wants to hold on to?
pr: Heavenly Father, I admit that I often want to stand by myself and forget to run to You. Tear down the high wall in my heart that I think keeps me safe, and teach me to choose humility before pride appears. In every shaking, let the first place I run be to Your name and Your presence. May Jesus truly be King in my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: The Lord is my strong tower. I run to him and I am safe.

t: You Are No Longer Who You Used to Be
v: We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.
For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will also be part of his resurrection;
knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.
For he who has died has been freed from sin.
But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him,
knowing that Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more. Death no longer has dominion over him!
For the death that he died, he died to sin one time; but the life that he lives, he lives to God.
Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Therefore don’t let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts.
b: This passage tells us plainly that a Christian is not a “slightly improved person” but one who has “died once and come alive again.” When we believed and were baptized, it was not just a religious ceremony but a change of life identity: the old self was crucified with Christ, and the new life began in the resurrection. Every step should have the pattern of new life, because we no longer belong to our old selves.

Paul keeps stressing “union with Christ.” It is not that we imitate Jesus by effort; Jesus’ death becomes our death, and Jesus’ resurrection becomes our life. Sin is no longer our master, and death no longer reigns. This is not a matter of feeling but a spiritual fact. Whether you feel weak or strong, the truth has already been declared: you have died to sin and are alive to God.

The key is in “consider yourselves.” Paul says to consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God. This is a choice of faith and a change of mindset. When we still see ourselves through the eyes of the old self, we easily let sin reign again; but when we see ourselves through God’s eyes, we can let Jesus rule our life. This is the selfless life: no longer letting the old self be king, but letting Christ live in me.
a: Define yourself by the truth
Remind yourself daily: I have died and risen with Christ and am no longer bound by old habits and an old identity.
Do not let sin be enthroned again
When temptation comes, do not just grit your teeth; declare, “This is no longer my master. Jesus is King.”
Live under the guidance of new life
Deliberately obey the Holy Spirit’s promptings, so that the pattern of new life is seen in daily living.
q: Today, am I looking at myself through the eyes of the old self, or living by my new identity in Christ?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for making me die and live with Christ. Renew my eyes, so that I am no longer defined by past sins and failures. Help me deny myself daily and let Jesus be King in me, that I may live out the pattern of new life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I have died and lived with Christ. Sin no longer reigns as my king; Jesus rules in my life.

t: Criticized as a Waste, Called a Beautiful Thing by Jesus
v: Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper,
a woman came to him having an alabaster jar of very expensive ointment, and she poured it on his head as he sat at the table.
But when his disciples saw this, they were indignant, saying, “Why this waste?
For this ointment might have been sold for much and given to the poor.”
However, knowing this, Jesus said to them, “Why do you trouble the woman? She has done a good work for me.
For you always have the poor with you, but you don’t always have me.
For in pouring this ointment on my body, she did it to prepare me for burial.
Most certainly I tell you, wherever this Good News is preached in the whole world, what this woman has done will also be spoken of as a memorial of her.”
b: What this woman did looked “irrational,” “too wasteful” and “impractical” to those around her. The disciples’ reaction was actually reasonable: by worldly values, the ointment could indeed be turned into many good deeds. But Jesus saw it with entirely different eyes. He said, it is a beautiful thing. She was not calculating cost but answering love; she was not putting on a show but simply giving the most precious thing to Jesus.

Jesus pointed out a spiritual key: not every “seemingly right thing” is better than “the thing that obeys Jesus at this moment.” The disciples thought of long-term charity; the woman saw Jesus in front of her. She seized a moment that could never come again and answered the Lord with whole-hearted love. This is a selfless heart, leaving itself no way out and offering no defense against others’ opinions, simply letting Jesus be King.

Jesus went further and said this deed would be told and become part of the gospel. It was not because of how expensive the ointment was but because her heart was wholly aimed at him. What God remembers is often not grand ministry but whether, at a critical moment, we gave the most precious thing to the Lord. When the world says “what a waste,” Jesus says, “a beautiful thing.”
a: Keep the best for Jesus
Do not give the Lord only leftover time, energy and love. Practice offering the most precious first.
Do not be held hostage by others’ opinions
Obeying Jesus’ decision may not be understood, but the Lord values your motive and your love.
Seize the key spiritual moments
When the Holy Spirit moves you to respond to the Lord, do not delay or calculate; simply obey.
q: Is there a “most precious ointment” in my life that Jesus is inviting me to offer right now?
pr: Lord Jesus, give me a simple heart that loves You, not bound by worldly calculation nor limited by others’ eyes. Teach me to be willing and glad before You, to give You what is most precious, so that my life may be a beautiful thing in Your eyes. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am willing to give the most precious to Jesus, keeping nothing back for myself, only for the glory of the Lord.

t: Those Who Can Sleep Have the Lord’s Light in Their Hearts
v: Answer me when I call, God of my righteousness. Give me relief from my distress. Have mercy on me, and hear my prayer.
You sons of men, how long shall my glory be turned into dishonor? Will you love vanity and seek after falsehood? Selah.
But know that the LORD has set apart for himself him who is godly; The LORD will hear when I call to him.
Stand in awe, and don’t sin. Search your own heart on your bed, and be still. Selah.
Offer the sacrifices of righteousness. Put your trust in the LORD.
Many say, “Who will show us any good?” LORD, let the light of your face shine on us.
You have put gladness in my heart, more than when their grain and their new wine are increased.
In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you alone, LORD, make me live in safety.
b: David called out to God in distress, not because his circumstances had changed, but because he knew that what really makes a person stand is not an improvement in the situation but God’s answer. He looked back and admitted that God had “set him free” when he was pressed; life does not get narrower and narrower but has a way out in God. This is a heart that does not rely on vindicating itself or on circumstances turning around, but relies only on “the God of my righteousness.”

Facing the shame, vanity and malice of others, David did not fight back in the flesh but declared a spiritual fact: the Lord has set apart for himself the godly. This is not self-comfort but a positioning of faith. He knew he belonged to God and that God heard his cry. So he chose, in the quiet of night on his bed, to search himself, be still, and not let emotions sin, bringing his heart back before God. This is the practice of selflessness: handing sovereignty back to God and letting Jesus be King.

Finally David gives a testimony that overturns the world’s values: the joy God gives is greater than the joy of a harvest of grain and new wine. A person may be outwardly rich yet restless within; but when God lifts up the light of his face, the heart has true gladness and peace. So David could “lay down and sleep in peace.” It is not that all his problems were solved, but that he put everything in the Lord’s hands. One who can sleep in peace is one who has given himself to God.
a: Turn to God first in distress
Do not first explain or prove yourself. Cry out to God first, and let him be your righteousness.
Practice a quiet heart in the night
Before sleep, review your thoughts of the day, do not let anger go to bed with you, and give everything to the Lord.
Seek the joy that comes from God
Do not build security on harvests and achievements, but in God’s presence.
q: What has kept me awake lately: a problem in my circumstances, or a heart I have not yet given to God?
pr: Lord, You are the God who makes me live in safety. Shine Your light on my heart, so that in distress I still rely on You and at night I can be quiet before You. Teach me not to argue for myself or be gripped by emotion, but to let Jesus be King in my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I give everything to the Lord. I will lie down in peace, and I will live in safety.

t: The Noise Outside Is Really a War Inside
v: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.
You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.
You adulterers and adulteresses, don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Whoever therefore wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
Or do you think that the Scripture says in vain, “The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously”?
But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Lament, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.
b: James goes straight to the point: the real source of wars, conflicts and fights between people is not the other person or the circumstances but the desires within that have not been dealt with. The louder the fighting outside, the fiercer the struggle inside. When “self” wants to be king and desires want to be satisfied, a person will grab, fight and envy, and still not find true satisfaction.

James then takes the problem deeper: it is not that people do not ask, but that they ask in the wrong direction. People ask God, yet still center on “my pleasure, my enjoyment, my satisfaction.” God does not answer such prayer, because it is not trust but using him. When someone says he wants God while holding tightly to the world, he is “double-minded,” which is spiritually unfaithfulness; friendship with the world is enmity with God.

But God does not leave people in despair. The turn in the passage is grace: “He gives more grace.” The way out is not suppressing ourselves by willpower but humbly returning to God. Submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, cleanse the heart, and let Jesus be King again. When a person is willing to humble himself before the Lord, God himself lifts him up, relationships are healed and life is set free.
a: Stop and deal with the inner battlefield first
In every conflict ask yourself: am I being pushed by desire now, or led by the Holy Spirit?
Adjust the focus of your prayer
Not only ask “what do I want?” but “Lord, what do You want?” so that prayer moves from using God to being toward God.
Choose humility, not opposition
Let go of the heart that wants to win, let Jesus be King in the relationship, and God’s grace begins to work.
q: In the most recent conflict that unsettled me, was the real root in the other person, or in a desire within me that I have not let go of?
pr: Lord, I admit that many times the war outside is really the confusion inside me. Today I am willing to humble myself before You and let go of the heart that wants to control, prove and be satisfied. Cleanse my hands and cleanse my heart, so that I draw near to You alone, and let Jesus reign again as King in my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I humble myself before the Lord, and God will make me stand firm by his grace.

t: It Is Not You Holding On to God; He Brings You Back With Love
v: “At that time,” says the LORD, “I will be the God of all the families of Israel, and they will be my people.”
The LORD says, “The people who survive the sword found favor in the wilderness; even Israel, when I went to cause him to rest.”
The LORD appeared of old to me, saying, “Yes, I have loved you with an everlasting love. Therefore I have drawn you with loving kindness.
I will build you again, and you will be built, O virgin of Israel. You will again be adorned with your tambourines, and will go out in the dances of those who make merry.
For the LORD says, “Sing with gladness for Jacob, and shout for the chief of the nations. Publish, praise, and say, ‘LORD, save your people, the remnant of Israel!’

Behold, I will bring them from the north country, and gather them from the uttermost parts of the earth, along with the blind and the lame, the woman with child and her who travails with child together. They will return as a great company.

They will come with weeping. I will lead them with petitions. I will cause them to walk by rivers of waters, in a straight way in which they won’t stumble; for I am a father to Israel. Ephraim is my firstborn.
b: This passage does not begin with human faithfulness but with God taking the initiative. Israel went through the sword, exile and wilderness, yet God said, “At that time, I will be the God of all the families.” It was not because they deserved it but because God first made the covenant, first chose and first loved. People who find grace in the wilderness often do so not because they walked the right road but because, when there was no road left, they were kept and preserved by God.

God himself spoke a stirring word: “I have loved you with an everlasting love.” This is not a passing emotion, nor a love that depends on performance, but a covenant love that is never withdrawn and never regretted. God does not pull people back with scolding but draws them back with loving kindness. True repentance is never forced; it is melted by love.

Even more wonderful, those God promises to bring back are not the strong and complete but the blind, the lame, the weeping and the weak. God himself leads them on a straight road where they will not stumble, because the key is not the strength of their feet but the Father’s love. This God is not a cold ruler but says, “I am a father to Israel.” The road home may be walked in tears, but it will surely be reached.
a: Believe again in God’s love in failure
Do not define God’s heart by your performance. His love for you has never grown shorter.
Let loving kindness bring you back
Not by scolding yourself, but by letting God’s love draw you to turn to him again.
Accept a life led by God’s pace
Admit your weakness and let the Father take you by the hand, no longer holding on by your own strength.
q: Am I trying hard to walk back to God on my own, or willing to let him bring me back by his loving kindness?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for loving me with an everlasting love. When I am weak, lost and in tears, You did not give up on me but personally drew and led me. Today I am willing to put down my pride in showing strength, simply return to You, let You be my Father, and let You lead me back onto the straight road of peace. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am one who is drawn by everlasting love and brought back personally by my Heavenly Father.

t: Not Bold Words About Dying for Him, but a Life of Loving One Another
v: When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him.
If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and he will glorify him immediately.
Little children, I will be with you a little while longer. You will seek me, and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you can’t come,’ so now I tell you.
A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”
Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered, “Where I am going, you can’t follow now, but you will follow afterwards.”
Peter said to him, “Lord, why can’t I follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”
Jesus answered him, “Will you lay down your life for me? Most certainly I tell you, the rooster won’t crow until you have denied me three times.
b: When Judas left the table and night truly fell, Jesus said, “Now the Son of Man is glorified.” To human eyes it was betrayal, failure, and the beginning of the cross; in God’s eyes it was the hour of glory. True glory is not being lifted up, but obeying the Father’s will completely; it is not protecting oneself, but giving oneself away in love. With his own life, Jesus showed us what it means to “let God be God and let the Father receive the glory.”

Then Jesus did not leave behind complicated doctrines or grand strategies, only “a new commandment”: love one another. This commandment is new not because the words were heard for the first time, but because the standard has been made completely new: “Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.” It is no longer a matter of loving by our own ability, but of letting Christ’s love live out through us. This is the life of selflessness: it is not that I try hard to love, but that Christ loves people within me.

Peter immediately declared great passion and determination, saying he was willing to die for the Lord. But Jesus saw deeper. He knew that people cannot stand by their own strength. Peter’s problem was not that he did not love the Lord, but that he trusted himself too much. True discipleship does not rest on a moment of fervor, but on learning to abide in the Lord, to be led by the Holy Spirit, and to let love become everyday life. Jesus did not reject Peter, but gently showed him that the road of laying down one’s life must begin with laying down the self.
a: Let love be the clearest mark of a disciple
It is not ability, eloquence, or zeal, but loving one another that lets people see Jesus.
Lay down your own fervor and vows
Admit your limits, learn to rely on the Lord, and let Christ live in you.
Practice self-giving love in daily relationships
At home, in church, and in ministry, choose to forgive, to bear with others, and to give.
q: Am I following the Lord now by my own resolve, or am I letting Christ’s love lead me from within?
pr: Lord Jesus, thank You for glorifying the Father through Your self-giving love. Save me from a life that relies on my own zeal and promises, and teach me selflessness so that You live in me. Holy Spirit, guide me to live out love for one another in my relationships every day, so that people may know I belong to You as Your disciple. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I do not follow the Lord by my own fervor, but let Christ’s love live out in me.

t: When You Lay Yourself Down, Relationships Are Healed
v: Jacob lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold, Esau was coming, and with him four hundred men. He divided the children between Leah, Rachel, and the two servants.
He put the servants and their children in front, Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear.
He himself passed over in front of them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.
Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept.
He lifted up his eyes, and saw the women and the children; and said, “Who are these with you?” He said, “The children whom God has graciously given your servant.”
Then the servants came near with their children, and they bowed themselves.
Leah also and her children came near, and bowed themselves. After them, Joseph came near with Rachel, and they bowed themselves.
Esau said, “What do you mean by all this company which I met?” Jacob said, “To find favor in the sight of my lord.”
Esau said, “I have enough, my brother; let that which you have be yours.”
Jacob said, “Please, no, if I have now found favor in your sight, then receive my present at my hand, because I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God, and you were pleased with me.
b: This is one of the most moving scenes of reconciliation in the Bible. Jacob had used trickery to take his brother’s birthright and blessing, and had been forced to flee for twenty years. Now he faces Esau again. He expected revenge, but met running feet, an embrace, and tears. The turnaround in the relationship did not begin with Esau; it had already happened in Jacob’s heart.

Jacob no longer stays at the back calculating; he walks to the very front. He no longer grasps for blessing; he bows to the ground seven times. This is not technique, but a changed life. In the previous chapter he wrestled with God at the ford of the Jabbok and was touched on the hip socket, and from then on he no longer relied on his own strength. Now he faces people with that same posture. Selflessness brought him back to his rightful place as a human being, and let God work in human hearts himself.

The most pivotal line is what Jacob says to Esau: “I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God.” This is not flattery, but true spiritual vision. When a person is willing to lay themselves down, no longer grasping for power or fighting over who is right, the other person is no longer just “the one who hurt me,” but becomes a channel through which God’s grace arrives. God’s presence is often revealed in relationships that have been healed.

Esau’s response also shows the fruit of healing. He says, “I have enough.” No more comparing, no more competing. Two brothers who were once torn apart over a blessing meet again in contentment and gratitude. It turns out that true blessing is not getting more, but having relationships restored.
a: Step courageously to the front, no longer hiding behind defenses
The first step toward reconciliation is often not waiting for the other person to change, but being willing to lay myself down first.
Choose humility in conflict instead of proving yourself
Bowing down is not defeat; it is a sign of letting God be King.
See people with spiritual eyes
When you see God at work in the other person’s life, an enemy can become a vessel of grace.
q: Is there a relationship in my life that has not been healed because I am still holding on to myself?
pr: Lord, thank You for working first in Jacob’s life before bringing the brothers together. Shine Your light on me, and let me see the pride, defensiveness, and hurt I still cling to. Help me lay myself down and return to my rightful place, so that You may be God and King. May You heal relationships and release grace through me. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: When I lay myself down, God personally heals my relationships.

t: Not Trying Harder, but Starting Over
v: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.
He came to Jesus by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher who has come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him.”
Jesus answered him, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom.”
Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”
Jesus answered, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born of water and Spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom.
That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit.
Nicodemus answered him, “How can these things be?”
Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel, and don’t understand these things?
As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up,
that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
One who believes in the Son has eternal life, but one who disobeys the Son won’t see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.”
b: Nicodemus was a man who “had everything”: position, learning, religious zeal, and moral standing. Yet he came to Jesus at night, which shows that deep down he knew all of this was still not enough. Jesus did not praise his efforts. He went straight to the heart of the problem: “Unless one is born anew, he can’t see the Kingdom of God.” Not patching up, not improving, but a change in the very source of life.

Nicodemus’s confusion is real: “How can a man be born when he is old?” It is a thought we often share, too: my character is set, my habits are long-standing, my life has gone this far; can I still change? Jesus’s answer shifts the focus from “Can a person?” to “Can God?” New birth is not entering the womb a second time, but the Holy Spirit giving a brand-new starting point for life within. What is born of the flesh can only live in the old self; what is born of the Spirit makes new life possible.

Jesus then used the picture of the serpent lifted up in the wilderness to show that the key to new birth lies not in what we do, but in “looking.” In those days the Israelites were not saved by an antidote or by merit; they only had to look at the bronze serpent lifted up, and they lived. It is the same today: not religious performance, but simply trusting in Jesus, who was lifted up and crucified. Faith is the doorway to a changed life; without faith, no amount of effort changes where we stand.

This passage reminds us that entering the Kingdom of God is not about “doing better,” but about “being born once.” Believing in Jesus is not just believing a set of teachings, but letting him become the new source of your life.
a: Stop merely trying to “improve yourself”
Ask yourself: have I been trying to become better through effort, without truly letting the Holy Spirit renew me?
Simply look to Jesus
Like the people in the wilderness, turn your eyes from yourself to the cross.
Accept that life can begin again
Whatever your age, background, or failures, it is never too late to be born again.
q: What do I rely on most right now: my own effort, or the salvation Jesus has accomplished?
pr: Lord Jesus, I admit that I often try to bring change through effort, while overlooking that what I truly need is new birth. Renew me by the Holy Spirit, so that I no longer live in the cycle of the old self, but in the new life You give. I want to look to You, the Savior lifted up, and trust in You alone. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I do not enter God’s Kingdom by effort, but receive new life through Jesus.

t: The Years That Were Lost, God Himself Restores
v: Land, don’t be afraid. Be glad and rejoice, for the LORD has done great things.
Don’t be afraid, you animals of the field; for the pastures of the wilderness spring up, for the tree bears its fruit. The fig tree and the vine yield their strength.

“Be glad then, you children of Zion, and rejoice in the LORD, your God; for he gives you the early rain in just measure, and he causes the rain to come down for you, the early rain and the latter rain, as before.
The threshing floors will be full of wheat, and the vats will overflow with new wine and oil.
I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the great locust, the grasshopper, and the caterpillar, my great army, which I sent among you.
You will have plenty to eat and be satisfied, and will praise the name of the LORD, your God, who has dealt wondrously with you; and my people will never again be disappointed.
You will know that I am among Israel, and that I am the LORD, your God, and there is no one else; and my people will never again be disappointed.
b: The background of this passage is Israel’s experience of a terrible plague of locusts and desolation. It was no small loss, but the collapse of a whole nation: the land laid waste, food cut off, no hope in sight for the future. Yet in that very moment of desolation, God did not stop at judgment, but took the initiative to declare comfort and restoration.

God first speaks to the “land” and the “animals of the field,” as if all of creation is included in his plan of redemption. This reminds us that restoration does not happen only in the human heart, but begins at the foundation, in our surroundings, and in every dimension of life. When God moves, barren ground sprouts again and dry seasons are renewed.

The most astonishing sentence is God’s own word: “I will restore to you the years that the locust has eaten.” God does not merely say, “It will be better in the future,” but points straight to past losses. The years that were devoured, the time that was wasted, the work that was destroyed are not permanent regrets in God’s hands. Restoration is not only a recovery in quantity, but a restoration of dignity and identity: “My people will never again be disgraced.”

The destination of this promise is not only harvest, but a rebuilt relationship: “You will know that I am in the midst of Israel.” True revival is not only that circumstances get better, but that we are reassured again that God is still with me and I still belong to him.
a: Give the past to God
The years you think are “too late” are in God’s hands, and he is able to restore them.
Choose to trust before the restoration comes
Don’t wait for circumstances to change before you rejoice; rejoice now because of God’s promise.
Let shame stop at God’s promise
God says “never again be disgraced,” so stop defining yourself by the past.
q: Which of my “years eaten by the locust” have I not yet handed over to God?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, You see what I have lost, missed, and had taken from me. Today I take hold of Your promise, believing that You heal not only the future but can also restore the past. Free me from living in shame and regret, and let me stand up again in Your presence. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: The years that were lost are not in the hands of the locusts, but in the hands of the God who restores.

t: Not Taking Advantage, but Living Through It Together
v: “‘If your brother has become poor, and his hand can’t support himself among you, then you shall uphold him. He shall live with you like an alien and a temporary resident.
