Take no interest from him or profit; but fear your God, that your brother may live among you.
You shall not lend him your money at interest, nor give him your food for profit.
I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, to give you the land of Canaan, and to be your God.
“‘If your brother has grown poor among you, and sells himself to you, you shall not make him to serve as a slave.
As a hired servant, and as a temporary resident, he shall be with you; he shall serve with you until the Year of Jubilee.
Then he shall go out from you, he and his children with him, and shall return to his own family, and to the possession of his fathers.
For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. They shall not be sold as slaves.
You shall not rule over him with harshness, but shall fear your God.
b: This passage uncovers something very important in God’s heart: among God’s people, “poverty” is not an opportunity to exploit someone, but a call to carry one another. God does not say, “Judge why he became poor,” but, “You shall uphold him.” In God’s Kingdom, brothers and sisters are not competitors, but a family living through it together. Truly fearing God is shown not in words, but in how you treat someone who has nothing in hand.

God specifically forbids “taking advantage of someone in need.” Whether it is lending money at interest or lending food for profit, the essence is the same: using another person’s hardship to increase one’s own gain. In the world this may look shrewd, but in God’s eyes it denies who God is. For God reminds his people: you were once slaves who were brought out. If we forget that we were saved by grace, it is easy to become cold toward others in their weakness.

Going deeper, God cares not only about temporary provision but also about a person’s dignity. Even if someone loses their freedom for a time because of poverty, in God’s eyes he is still not “merchandise,” but “my servant.” The establishment of the Jubilee lets people know that hardship is not forever, identity is not erased, and the future can still return to the inheritance God originally gave. God does not allow his people to use power or systems to keep someone at the bottom for life.
a: When I have the means, do I lift people up or take advantage?
Fearing God leads us to choose compassion in another’s need, rather than calculation.
Before seeing others, remember where you came from
We are all people God brought out of “Egypt”; not one of us stands by our own strength.
Give people hope instead of labels
Don’t define a person’s whole life by a moment of hardship; God keeps a way of restoration open for them.
q: When others fall into weakness, is my attitude more like “family,” or like “master”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You do not set our worth by our circumstances, but by salvation determine our identity. Adjust my vision so that, in others’ need, I see Your heart rather than my own advantage. Let me be someone who helps people live, not someone who makes their burdens heavier. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I do not find security by pushing others down; I live out grace by fearing God.

t: Faith Is Not a Slogan, but Being Led by the Lord Every Day
v: But we beg you, brothers, to know those who labor among you, and are over you in the Lord and admonish you,
and to respect and honor them in love for their work’s sake. Be at peace among yourselves.
We exhort you, brothers: Admonish the disorderly; encourage the faint-hearted; support the weak; be patient toward all.
See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone, but always follow after that which is good for one another and for all.
Always rejoice.
Pray without ceasing.
In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.
Don’t quench the Spirit.
Don’t despise prophecies.
Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.
Abstain from every form of evil.
May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely. May your whole spirit, soul, and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
b: This passage shows us that faith does not happen only in worship or on the pulpit, but is lived out in our daily relationships and choices. Paul begins with how we get along with one another: respecting spiritual leaders, living at peace, supporting the weak, being patient with everyone. Spiritual maturity is not about how high you stand, but whether you are willing to bend down and treat people with the heart of Jesus.

Then Paul boils spiritual life down to three practices that look simple but run very deep: always rejoice, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in everything. This does not demand that we stay emotionally high all the time, but reminds us that the lordship of our life lies not in circumstances but in Jesus. When we live selflessly, not propping ourselves up but letting the Holy Spirit lead and relying on the Lord with our hearts, we can stay connected to God in any state.

Finally, Paul points out that true sanctification does not come from human willpower, but from “the God of peace himself” at work. We are to stay sensitive to the Holy Spirit, not quenching his prompting, yet not following blindly either, but testing in truth and holding fast to what is good. The whole life, inside and out, is kept by God until the Lord returns. Faith is not held up by us; it is God leading us by the hand all the way.
a: Live out Christ in your relationships
Today, deliberately respond to people with gentleness, patience, and goodness rather than instinctive reaction.
Build three rhythms of spiritual life
Practice joy, prayer, and thanksgiving, so your heart returns to Jesus every day.
Keep a soft heart toward the Holy Spirit
Don’t ignore his promptings, and don’t rely on your own judgment; let God’s word guide your choices.
q: Does my faith right now stay in my thoughts, or does it truly shape how I live and how I treat people each day?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You that You not only called me to believe, but also personally teach me how to live. Help me live out the life of Jesus in my relationships, and rely on the Holy Spirit rather than myself in everything. May You personally guard my heart and mind, so that I walk all my life in Your peace and truth until the Lord Jesus returns. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I live each day relying on the Lord, letting Jesus be King in my life until he returns.

t: When Your Heart Is Parched, Don’t Pretend to Be Strong; Turn to God
v: Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing?
My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. When shall I come and appear before God?
My tears have been my food day and night, while they continually ask me, “Where is your God?”
These things I remember, and pour out my soul within me, how I used to go with the crowd, and led them to God’s house, with the voice of joy and praise, a multitude keeping a holy day.
Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God! For I shall still praise him for the saving help of his presence.
My God, my soul is in despair within me. Therefore I remember you from the land of the Jordan, the heights of Hermon, from the hill Mizar.
Deep calls to deep at the noise of your waterfalls. All your waves and your billows have swept over me.
The LORD will command his loving kindness in the daytime. In the night his song shall be with me: a prayer to the God of my life.
I will ask God, my rock, “Why have you forgotten me? Why do I go mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?”
As with a sword in my bones, my adversaries reproach me, while they continually ask me, “Where is your God?”
Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God! For I shall still praise him, the saving help of my countenance, and my God.
b: This psalm does not pretend to be spiritually strong; it honestly shows a heart that is deeply parched, weeping, and questioned. The psalmist does not disbelieve in God; he longs for God deeply, yet cannot feel God’s presence for a time. True faith is not never being in a low place, but still crying out to God in the low place. Longing like a deer for streams of water is a life-instinct cry, with no performance and no packaging, only the most honest need for God.

The psalmist asks himself again and again: “Why are you in despair, my soul?” This is not a rebuke, but a spiritual self-dialogue. He does not sink along with his emotions, but brings his heart back to the right focus: “Hope in God.” This is not persuading oneself to be optimistic with the mind, but choosing with the heart to hand sovereignty back to God and let God be King. Even if feelings have not changed and circumstances have not shifted, faith first stands back in its rightful place.

More precious still, even while weeping the psalmist declares: “In the daytime the Lord will command his loving kindness; in the night his song will be with me.” This is a selfless kind of trust: not defining God by feelings, but being held up by God’s faithfulness. He knows that though the waves sweep over him, loving kindness has never left. God is not only the God who saves him, but the glory of his face, the God who is with him even in the dark of night.
a: Honestly face the thirst in your heart
Don’t suppress it or pretend; bring your true heart before God.
Practice spiritual dialogue in your emotions
Don’t be led around by feelings; remind yourself to hope in God.
Choose to draw near to God even in the night
Even when you feel nothing, keep praying and worshiping.
q: When my heart is troubled and restless, do I let my emotions be king, or do I bring my heart back to God?
pr: Heavenly Father, You know the thirst in my heart and my tears. Thank You for not despising my weak cry. When I feel that You are far away, draw my heart to look to You again. Help me not to define You by my feelings, but to acknowledge by faith that You still reign and still love me. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Even in thirst and in the dark of night, I still hope in God, for he is the help and glory of my life.

t: Not Striving to Love, but Dwelling in Being Loved
v: We know and have believed the love which God has for us. God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.
In this, love has been made perfect among us, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment, because as he is, even so we are in this world.
There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. He who fears is not made perfect in love.
We love him, because he first loved us.
If a man says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?
This commandment we have from him, that he who loves God should also love his brother.
b: This passage does not begin with “how you should love,” but first declares a foundational truth: “We know and have believed the love which God has in us.” True love does not begin with human effort, but with believing in God’s love. When a person dwells in God’s love, not just occasionally remembering that God loves me but making this love the home of their life, God lives in them, and life is naturally changed.

John goes on to point out that perfect love brings a result: boldness without fear. The root of fear is not circumstances, but uncertainty about love; when the heart still feels it needs to be condemned or punished, it means it has not yet truly rested in God’s love. But when we let Jesus be King and receive the salvation he has already accomplished, love slowly matures in us, and we no longer live in fear, but in the identity of children.

Finally, this love that comes from God will surely flow toward people. Not because our brothers and sisters are lovable, but because we were loved first. If we only say with our mouths that we love God, yet our relationships are full of coldness, resentment, and separation, it means God’s love has not yet truly taken charge. Loving God will certainly transform our attitude toward people, so that we live out the life of Christ in our daily relationships.
a: First rest in the fact that God loves you
Remind yourself every day: it was not I who loved God first, but God who already loved me.
Let love replace fear as king
When fear arises, choose to return to God’s love rather than propping yourself up.
Practice visible love in your relationships
Respond to the people around you with actions, forgiveness, and patience.
q: Right now, am I striving to prove I am worthy to be loved, or truly dwelling in the love God has already given me?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for loving me first, accepting me when I was still weak and imperfect. Help me no longer be ruled by fear, but rest in Your love. Let this love mature in my life, and flow naturally to the people around me. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I dwell in God’s love, am not bound by fear, and let love reign in my life.

t: Not Who I Am, but Whom I Live For
v: This is John’s testimony, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?”
He declared, and didn’t deny, but he declared, “I am not the Christ.”
They asked him, “What then? Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the prophet?” He answered, “No.”
They said therefore to him, “Who are you? Give us an answer to take back to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”
He said, “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said.”
The ones who had been sent were from the Pharisees.
They asked him, “Why then do you baptize if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?”
John answered them, “I baptize in water, but among you stands one whom you don’t know.
He is the one who comes after me, who is preferred before me, whose sandal strap I’m not worthy to loosen.”
These things were done in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
b: The focus of this passage is not on who John is, but on the fact that he knows clearly “who he is not.” When the crowd kept pressing him about his identity, status, and role, John without hesitation denied every title that might have lifted him up: “I am not the Christ.” He was in no hurry to prove himself, and did not use the moment to build a name; again and again he moved the focus away from himself. This is a very deep humility: knowing he is not the main character, yet gladly standing in the place God entrusted to him.

John defined his whole life in one sentence: “the voice in the wilderness.” The nature of a voice is not to be seen but to be heard; not to point to itself, but to the one who is coming. This is a portrait of the selfless life: not taking the stage, only fulfilling the mission. John did not try to become the light; he chose to prepare the way for the light, so that Jesus would be King and people would see the true Savior.

Finally, John says something deeply striking: “Among you stands one whom you don’t know.” Many were busy identifying spiritual figures, yet missed Jesus standing right in front of them. John reminds us that true spiritual service is not getting people to know me, but helping people recognize Jesus. When we are willing to humble ourselves, the Holy Spirit can bring people to Christ through us.
a: Let go of the urge to prove yourself
Rest in your identity and role, knowing that the place God has given you is enough.
Gladly be someone who points to Jesus
Don’t grab the spotlight; just faithfully walk the stretch of road God has entrusted to you.
Make straight the Lord’s way in daily life
Through your life, attitude, and choices, prepare hearts to meet Jesus.
q: Right now, do I care more about “what others think of me,” or about “whether people see Jesus more clearly because of me”?
pr: Lord Jesus, thank You for being the true light that shines on my life. Help me, like John the Baptist, not to exalt myself, but simply to prepare the way for You. Let all my words and actions point to You, so that people may meet You and know You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am not the main character; I am one who prepares the way for Jesus. May he be exalted in my life.

t: The One Who Was Overlooked Carried My Whole Life
v: Who has believed our message? To whom has the LORD’s arm been revealed?
For he grew up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of dry ground. He has no good looks or majesty. When we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.
He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
b: This passage shows us a profound contrast: what people see as “unexpected” is the salvation God had already prepared. This suffering servant had no striking appearance and no attractive qualities; he was even despised and rejected. But it is precisely in such lowliness that the arm of the Lord is revealed. God’s power has never come through outward glory, but through self-giving love.

More astonishing still, everything he bore was not his own problem, but the problem of our lives. The text insists again and again on “our”: our sickness, our suffering, our transgressions, our iniquities. We thought he was struck by God, but in fact he willingly stood in the sinner’s place and let the punishment fall on himself, so that we might have peace. This is completely selfless love, the way of the cross on which Jesus is King.

The last line lays out the human condition plainly: “All we like sheep have gone astray; everyone has turned to his own way.” The problem is not just occasional stumbling, but that life’s direction has gone wrong. But God did not leave us to be lost; he laid the sin of us all on him. It is not that we took hold of God, but that Jesus stood on the cross and carried the lost ones back, one by one.
a: Never take the love of the cross lightly
Remind yourself every day that the peace I have today was bought with Jesus’s life.
Look to the suffering Lord in your weakness
When you are overlooked, misunderstood, or crushed, remember that Jesus has already walked this road.
Hand back to the Lord a heart that goes its own way
Stop being your own master, and be willing to return to the Shepherd’s leading.
q: Do I truly believe that what Jesus bore is the deepest need of my whole life?
pr: Lord Jesus, thank You for being willing to be despised and rejected in order to rescue me from being lost. When I look at the cross, keep me from ever making light of this love that cost so much. Today I want to hand to You my sin, my pain, and my direction, and let You be King in my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Because Jesus was wounded for me and bore it for me, in him I have peace and healing.

t: It Is Not Rules That Bind You, but God Who Gives You Freedom
v: God spoke all these words, saying,
“I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.
“You shall have no other gods before me.
“You shall not make for yourselves an idol, nor any image of anything that is in the heavens above, or that is on the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
“You shall not misuse the name of the LORD your God, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who misuses his name.
“Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
“Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the LORD your God gives you.
“You shall not murder.
“You shall not commit adultery.
“You shall not steal.
“You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.
“You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor’s.”
b: This passage is often misunderstood as “a pile of things you can’t do,” but before God gave the commandments, he said one key sentence: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the house of bondage.” In other words, the commandments are not the condition for being saved, but the way of life after being set free. God did not first demand that people keep rules before loving them; he first rescued people from bondage, and then taught them how not to go back into slavery.

The first half of the Ten Commandments points to our relationship with God. Having only one God, not misusing his name, and keeping the Sabbath are not about religious form at their core, but about letting God truly sit at the center of our lives. When there is another god in the heart, something that replaces God, life will once again be controlled. The Sabbath is not a burden; it reminds us that we do not hold up the world by ourselves, but let God be King and let the heart return to rest.

The second half concerns relationships between people. Do not murder, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, or covet: these are not suppressing human nature, but boundaries that protect life, relationships, and the soul. Coveting is not an outward behavior, but an inner desire to take God’s place. What God values is not surface law-keeping, but a heart that is not led around by desire and is willing to let him guide.
a: First remember that you are one who has been rescued
Remind yourself every day: I obey not to be accepted, but because I am already loved.
Let God sit at the center of your life
Examine whether anything in your heart has taken God’s place, and hand sovereignty back to Jesus.
Keeping boundaries is keeping freedom
In relationships and choices, choose what pleases God rather than following desire.
q: Is my obedience to God right now out of love and freedom, or out of pressure and reluctance?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for not pressing me down with the law, but first leading me out of sin and bondage. Help me understand that Your commandments come from love, to protect me and guide me to live in true freedom. Today I want to hand the sovereignty of my life to You, so that You are King and guide my choices every day. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am not a slave to the law, but one whom God has rescued and who lives out freedom in Christ.

t: When You See a Rainbow, Remember That God Has Not Forgotten You
v: God said, “This is the token of the covenant which I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for perpetual generations:
I set my rainbow in the cloud, and it will be a sign of a covenant between me and the earth.
When I bring a cloud over the earth, that the rainbow will be seen in the cloud,
I will remember my covenant, which is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh, and the waters will no more become a flood to destroy all flesh.
The rainbow will be in the cloud. I will look at it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth.”
b: This passage takes place after the flood. The world had been judged and destroyed, and humanity was full of unease and fear about the future. Against this background, God took the initiative to make a covenant, and not only with Noah, but with “you and every living creature that is with you.” This is a covenant of grace initiated by God, not one begged for or earned by human performance, but one God himself decided to keep.

What is especially precious is that the sign of this covenant is “for God to see.” God says, “I will look at it, that I may remember.” The rainbow is not only a comforting piece of scenery for people, but a reminder God sets for himself. When clouds cover the earth and the storm has not stopped, the rainbow appears against the darkest background, declaring that God’s faithfulness has not been swallowed up by circumstances. Even when people forget God in the chaos, God does not forget people.

The rainbow reminds us that God’s covenant is an “everlasting covenant.” It is not a short-term guarantee or a promise adjusted to circumstances. The human world will fail again and again, and the human heart is weak, yet God still declares through a sign: he remembers, he keeps covenant, he reigns. True peace is not that the storm disappears, but knowing that above the storm there is a God who keeps covenant and shows loving kindness.
a: Remember in the storm that God still reigns
When circumstances are unsteady and your mood is low, remind yourself: God’s covenant has not changed.
Let God’s faithfulness replace your fear
Don’t let past experiences of judgment define the future; believe God has made an everlasting covenant.
Respond in faith to God’s remembering
Since God has not forgotten you, choose every day to remember him and rely on him.
q: When clouds cover my life, am I gripped by fear, or willing to believe God still remembers me?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for placing a rainbow after the storm for me, so that I know You are a covenant-keeping God who does not change. When my heart is uneasy and I fear the future, help me remember Your promises and choose to trust You rather than be swayed by circumstances. Today I want to place my tomorrow in Your hands, because You have never forgotten me. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Even when clouds cover the sky, I still believe God remembers me and keeps his covenant forever.

t: Not a Formula Prayer, but Pressing Your Life Against Another’s
v: Gehazi went ahead of them, and laid the staff on the child’s face; but there was no voice and no hearing. Therefore he returned to meet him, and told him, “The child has not awakened.”
When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and lying on his bed.
He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to the LORD.
He went up and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the child’s flesh grew warm.
Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth, then went up and stretched himself out on him. Then the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.
b: This passage is deeply striking, and deeply real. Gehazi did everything “the right way,” laying the prophet’s staff on the child’s face, yet nothing happened. There was nothing wrong with the staff, and nothing wrong with the procedure, but life did not flow. This reminds us that spiritual things do not depend on outward form, nor on copying someone else’s success, but need life itself.

When Elisha arrived, he did not rush to show his power or perform a miracle before the crowd. He “shut the door,” leaving only himself and the child, and prayed to the Lord. True spiritual work often begins in places with no applause, no audience, and no shortcuts. Resurrection is not a performance; it costs something.

Deeper still, Elisha did not command from a distance, but pressed his whole self against the child: mouth to mouth, eyes to eyes, hands to hands. This is not technique, but self-giving; not a method, but the transmission of life. The child did not wake immediately, but his body “grew warm,” and life was coming back. Spiritual restoration is often like this: not an instant change, but a gradual warming.

At last the child sneezed seven times and opened his eyes. This was a resurrection wholly from God, yet the one God used was a servant willing to pay the price, willing to draw close to death, and willing to lay himself down. This also foreshadows Jesus: he did not save from a distance, but became flesh, entered our death, and brought true life.
a: Don’t just serve with methods, accompany with your life
People are truly restored not because you said the right words, but because you were willing to be present.
Don’t give up when you can’t see results
The child warmed first, and woke later; change in life takes a process, so don’t rush to judge.
Shut the door and go to God first
Before busying yourself with “doing something,” return first to prayer and God’s presence.
q: Lately, have I been solving problems with spiritual methods, or am I willing to truly lay my life down and let God use it?
pr: Heavenly Father, forgive me for so often wanting shortcuts to deal with life’s problems while unwilling to pay the price of presence and self-giving. Today I want to learn Elisha’s heart, to come before You in prayer first, and then let my life become a vessel through which You flow. Whether the change is fast or slow, bring life truly back. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I do not serve by method, but let God’s life flow through me and bring true resurrection.

t: Not Waiting for the Door to Open, but Tearing Up the Roof for Love
v: When he entered again into Capernaum after some days, it was heard that he was at home.
Immediately many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even around the door; and he spoke the word to them.
Four people came, carrying a paralytic to him.
When they could not come near to him for the crowd, they removed the roof where he was. When they had broken it up, they let down the mat that the paralytic was lying on.
Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven you.”
b: This passage gives us a deeply moving picture. Jesus was teaching inside the house, with a sea of people outside and the door packed shut. For a paralyzed man, this was a situation of “no way in”: he could not walk, could not squeeze through, could not fight for a chance on his own. But he had four friends, and they chose not to give up.

These four did not complain about the circumstances, blame the crowd, or say, “Maybe next time.” They made an extraordinary decision: tear up the roof. This was not impulse, but faith; not recklessness, but love. They believed that if they could just bring the man to Jesus, Jesus would surely have a way.

What Jesus saw was not only the paralytic’s need, but “their faith.” True faith is often not a slogan, but the action of a group of people willing to pay a price for one person. More wonderful still, Jesus did not heal his body first, but said, “Your sins are forgiven you.” For in Jesus’s eyes, the deepest paralysis is not legs that cannot walk, but a heart bound by sin and guilt.

This also reminds us: often what we need most is not a change in outward circumstances, but renewal at the core of our lives. When a person is truly forgiven, accepted, and restored, their whole life has the possibility of standing up again.
a: Be one of the four friends
Notice the people around you who “can’t move,” and bring them to Jesus through action.
Don’t let circumstances limit your faith
A closed door doesn’t mean God isn’t working; sometimes faith has to go up.
Trust that Jesus knows the real need
Entrust people to Jesus and let him decide which layer of life to deal with first.
q: Am I waiting for circumstances to change, or willing to go one step further for love, even to “tear up the roof”?
pr: Lord Jesus, thank You for letting me see that real faith does not stop at words but becomes action. Give me a heart willing to pay a price for others, not shrinking back from difficulty and not letting circumstances limit love. Heal also the deepest need in my life, so that I receive true freedom from the inside out. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am not limited by circumstances; I am willing to act in love and bring people to Jesus, to witness his power to forgive and renew.

t: It Is Not Whether You Qualify, but Whether You Will Call Out
v: For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, and is rich to all who call on him.
For, “Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.”
How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher?
And how will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things!”
b: This passage makes salvation both very clear and very gentle. Paul does not begin with human conditions, but declares one thing first: everyone has the same Lord. Regardless of background, past, failures, or achievements, there is no high or low before God. The only key is not “who you are,” but “whether you call on him.”

“Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.” This sentence tears down the biggest lie in the human heart: “I’ll come to God after I get a little better.” The truth is exactly the opposite. It is precisely when people have no way out and no strength to save themselves, and call on the Lord’s name, that they experience real rescue. Salvation is not a prize for the strong, but for those willing to admit their need.
But Paul also points out a spiritual chain: without hearing, there is no believing; without preaching, there is no hearing; without sending, no one is willing to go.

This means many people do not reject God; no one has ever brought the good news to them. So the gospel is not only the joyful news “I am saved,” but also the call “I am willing to be a channel.” God saves people, and God also sends people; God is generous to those who call on him, and he also uses those who are willing to go out for him.

“How beautiful are the feet” not because the feet are clean or the road is easy, but because those feet come carrying news of life. In God’s eyes, those willing to step out of their comfort zone for the gospel are precious indeed.
a: Simply call on the Lord’s name
Don’t wait until you are worthy; open yourself and call on the Lord today.
See the people around you who have not yet heard
Near or far, there are people waiting to hear the good news of the gospel.
Be willing to respond to being sent
Not everyone stands on a platform, but everyone can be a messenger.
q: Have I received salvation yet forgotten that there are people still waiting to “hear”?
pr: Lord, thank You for setting no threshold, but opening grace to all who call on You. Let me not stay only at being rescued, but be willing to respond to Your sending. Use my life, my words, and my steps to be a vessel that brings good news to people. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I boldly call on the Lord’s name, and am willing to respond to being sent, to be one who passes on the good news of salvation.

t: The Tighter You Grip, the More You Lose
v: There is one who scatters, and increases yet more. There is one who withholds more than is appropriate, but gains poverty.
The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.
People curse someone who withholds grain, but blessing will be on the head of him who sells it.
He who diligently seeks good seeks favor, but he who searches after evil, it shall come to him.
He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous shall flourish as the green leaf.
He who troubles his own house shall inherit the wind. The foolish shall be servant to the wise of heart.
The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life. He who is wise wins souls.
Behold, the righteous shall be repaid on the earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner!
b: This passage completely overturns human instinct. By human logic, “holding on is safe, and giving away means having less”; but God’s truth says: **the one who gives freely ends up with more; the one who grips too tightly ends up poorer.** Because what truly determines abundance is not how much you have, but whom you trust.

“He who waters shall be watered also himself” is not an investment formula, but a law of spiritual life. When a person is willing to be a channel, not bound by self and fear, God makes life flow like living water without ceasing. On the other hand, those who trust in their wealth seem secure, but have placed their security in the wrong place, and will eventually fall.

The text also reminds us that true poverty is not only having no money, but having no fruit of life. The fruit of the righteous is “a tree of life,” not cold resources, but life-influence that nourishes people; the wise are not only those who can get things done, but those who “win souls,” so that people receive life, hope, and direction through them.

Finally, God points out a serious yet righteous fact: the choices of life will surely bring results. God is not a bystander with folded arms, but a just Lord. How a person lives today and how they use what God has entrusted to them will be made plain, in this life and in eternity.
a: Practice the faith of letting go
Deliberately choose to give with your time, resources, or relationships, rather than only holding back.
Examine the source of your security
Do I rely on money, ability, or the God who supplies me?
Pursue a life that nourishes people
Don’t just do what is right; let people draw closer to God and have more life because of you.
q: What have I been gripping tightest lately? Has it replaced God as the security in my heart?
pr: Heavenly Father, shine Your light on me, and let me see whether I am gripping too tightly out of fear. Teach me to give, to refresh others, and to be a channel of blessing as You are. May I not rely on passing wealth, but trust in You alone, and live the life of a righteous person who bears the fruit of life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I choose to trust God rather than hold on to the world.

t: It Is Not You Holding Up Your Faith; God Stands Up for You
v: Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages who dwell in all the earth: “Peace be multiplied to you.

“I make a decree that in all the dominion of my kingdom men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel. “For he is the living God, and steadfast forever. His kingdom is that which will not be destroyed. His dominion will be even to the end.
He delivers and rescues. He works signs and wonders in heaven and in earth, who has delivered Daniel from the power of the lions.”
So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.
b: The main character of this passage seems to be Daniel, but it is really the God who personally testifies for Daniel. Daniel did not defend himself, did not turn the tables by force, and was not in a hurry to prove he was right; he simply stood faithfully before God. The result was not that Daniel spoke for God, but that God made a foreign king proclaim for him: he is the living God who endures forever.

Daniel was thrown into the lions’ den not because he had done wrong, but because he had done right. In the darkest, most helpless, most silenced situation, God was not absent. God did not merely give him one way out; he overturned the whole situation, silencing the enemies, giving the king a voice, and exalting God’s name throughout the earth.

Here is a deep reminder for us: true faith is not whether you can hold up under circumstances, but whether you are willing to place yourself in God’s hands. Daniel did not ask God to quickly change the system, and did not ask God to remove the lions; he just prayed as usual and feared God as usual. The result was that God personally protected, personally rescued, and personally vindicated him.

Finally, the text says Daniel “prospered.” This was not a brief season of smooth sailing, but prospering that stands firm and goes far in God’s Kingdom. Because he did not use his own methods to save his life, but let God be his security. When a person lets God be King, God himself takes responsibility for that person’s future.
a: Choose faithfulness under pressure
Don’t be in a hurry to escape; first ask: do I still fear God and refuse to compromise?
Hand your defense over to God
Don’t rush to prove yourself; let God speak for you at the right time.
Believe God can turn the situation around
Even if your circumstances are a lions’ den, God still reigns and is never out of control for a moment.
q: What do I most want to fight for on my own right now? Am I willing to leave the outcome to God rather than hold it up myself?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You that You are the living God who endures forever. When I am misunderstood, oppressed, or pushed to where there is no retreat, teach me, like Daniel, to fear You alone and not compromise. Today I place my situation, my reputation, and my future in Your hands, trusting that You will personally protect and rescue me, and bear witness for me at the right time. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I choose to fear God rather than rely on myself, and God will personally stand up for me.

t: The Healed Become a Blessing
v: Soon afterwards, he went about through cities and villages, preaching and bringing the good news of God’s Kingdom. With him were the twelve,
and certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary who was called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out;
and Joanna, the wife of Chuzas, Herod’s steward; Susanna; and many others who served them from their possessions.
b: This record is short, yet full of warmth. Jesus traveled through cities and villages proclaiming the good news of the Kingdom of God, and at his side were not only the disciples, but also a group of people who had once been healed.

They had been possessed by demons and burdened by illness; they were people on the margins of society, people who had once been broken. But when Jesus walked into their lives, darkness withdrew, chains loosened, and their identity was renewed. They were no longer merely “the healed,” but became “those who walk with the Lord.”

True change does not stop at the moment of being helped, but is a change in the direction of life. They did not stop at being moved; they chose to follow Jesus’s footsteps. They did not only receive grace; they began to supply grace. They served Jesus and the disciples out of their own possessions, which is a surrender of sovereignty: the Lord is not only my Savior, but also the King of my life.

The work of God’s Kingdom has never been held up by a few, but accomplished by many hearts willing to give themselves. Some stand in front and preach, some quietly support in the background; some go out to proclaim, some faithfully supply. When everyone lets Jesus be King, the whole community forms a healthy, flowing, mutually completing divine order.

This is the order of life: first life, then relationship, then ministry. They first experienced healing and built a relationship with the Lord, and then service flowed out naturally. Not to prove themselves by doing things, but because they were loved, so they were willing to give themselves. Not propped up by passion, but flowing from grace.
a: Look back on the Lord’s healing in me
Reflect on how the Lord has saved, turned around, and sustained me, and let gratitude be rekindled.
From receiving to supplying
Am I willing to make the time, money, and gifts God has given me a blessing to others?
Walk with the Lord instead of watching from afar
Don’t just be moved by the message, but truly throw yourself into the action of God’s Kingdom.
q: Am I still at the stage of “being helped,” or have I become someone who “blesses others”?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for healing and freeing me when I was at my weakest. Help me not merely to receive grace, but to become an outlet of grace. Let me gladly follow You and place my time, resources, and life in Your hands. May You reign as King in me, and make me part of the blessing of Your Kingdom. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Because the Lord has healed and saved me, I gladly walk with Jesus and become a blessing to others.

t: In Tribulation, Standing in Grace
v: Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ;
through whom we also have our access by faith into this grace in which we stand. We rejoice in hope of the glory of God.
Not only this, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance;
and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope;
and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.
b: This passage begins with a key: “justified by faith.” Salvation is not earned by works, but by trusting in Jesus and being declared righteous by God. When we have peace with God, life no longer lives under accusation and fear, but stands in grace. Not entering grace now and then, but “this grace in which we stand,” a firm position.

Deeper still, Paul says we can rejoice even in suffering. This is not denying pain, but knowing that God is at work. Tribulation is not the end, but a process. Suffering produces perseverance, perseverance shapes proven character, and proven character gives birth to hope. God does not immediately remove difficulty, but shapes us in it, making our lives more mature and more steady.

And the foundation of all this is that the Holy Spirit pours God’s love into our hearts. Not outward encouragement, but inward filling. When God’s love flows within the heart, hope will not come to nothing. Because we know that God has not left, and we are still standing in grace.
True victory is not having no tribulation, but still standing firm in the midst of it. Not by gritting our teeth on our own, but because God’s love in our hearts has become our strength.
a: Know your position
Remind yourself today: I am not standing in fear, but standing in grace.
See tribulation with heaven’s eyes
Treat hardship as a vessel that shapes life, not as evidence against yourself.
Let the Holy Spirit fill your heart
Pray often, and let God’s love be poured out again, so that hope is rekindled.
q: Facing my present difficulty, am I propping myself up on my own, or trusting that God is shaping hope within me?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for making me at peace with You through Jesus, and for letting me stand in grace. When tribulation comes, help me stand by faith and not by feelings. May the Holy Spirit pour Your love into my heart again, so that I never lose hope in any circumstance. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am justified by faith and stand in grace; in tribulation, I still have hope.

t: After Receiving Blessing, Guard Your First Love All the More
v: It shall be, when the LORD your God brings you into the land which he swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give you, great and goodly cities which you didn’t build,
and houses full of all good things which you didn’t fill, and cisterns dug out which you didn’t dig, vineyards and olive trees which you didn’t plant, and you shall eat and be full;
then beware lest you forget the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.
You shall fear the LORD your God; and you shall serve him, and shall swear by his name.
You shall not go after other gods, of the gods of the peoples who are around you,
for the LORD your God among you is a jealous God, lest the anger of the LORD your God be kindled against you, and he destroy you from off the face of the earth.
You shall not tempt the LORD your God, as you tempted him in Massah.
You shall diligently keep the commandments of the LORD your God, and his testimonies, and his statutes, which he has commanded you.
You shall do that which is right and good in the LORD’s sight, that it may be well with you and that you may go in and possess the good land which the LORD swore to your fathers,
to thrust out all your enemies from before you, as the LORD has spoken.
b: These words were not spoken to people in the wilderness, but to those “about to enter a land of abundance.” God reminded them: you are going to live in cities you did not build, enjoy vineyards you did not plant, and drink water from wells you did not dig. All of this is grace.

Yet the real danger lies not in lack, but in fullness. People often hold tightly to God in hardship, yet slowly forget him in abundance. When life is stable, resources are plentiful, and career is successful, the heart easily credits itself, and may even turn to other things for support.
So God says, “Then beware lest you forget.” Forgetting is the starting point of spiritual decline. It is not leaving God overnight, but slowly losing reverence in the course of daily life.
God is a jealous God, and he wants us to belong to him alone. Not because he is petty, but because he knows that when we follow other gods, what we lose in the end is not God, but ourselves.
True enjoyment of blessing is not only entering the good land, but still fearing God and walking in his ways in the good land. When a person guards their first love, blessing can last.
a: Count your blessings in times of ease
Deliberately think today: how much of what I have did God give me freely?
Keep reverence in times of fullness
Don’t wait until you lose something to pray; let reverence become a daily habit.
Guard blessing with obedience
In every choice ask: is this right and good in the sight of the Lord?
q: When life is stable and going well, does my heart draw closer to God, or rely more on myself?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for giving me many blessings I did not plant. Guard my heart, so that I do not forget You in times of ease and still fear You in fullness. Let me never turn aside from Your way all my life, and truly live in Your grace and the good land You give. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Whether in lack or abundance, I fear the Lord and guard my first love for God.

t: Live a Life Worthy of Your Calling
v: I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called,
with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love,
being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
There is one body and one Spirit, even as you also were called in one hope of your calling,
one Lord, one faith, one baptism,
one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in us all.
But to each one of us, the grace was given according to the measure of the gift of Christ.
b: Paul wrote these words from a prison cell. He was not teaching theory; he was proving the truth with his life. He says, “Walk worthily of the calling with which you were called.”
Faith is not a label of identity; it is a way of life. Since our heavenly Father has called us to be his children, our lives should reflect that honor.

This “worthy walk” shows up first in our relationships: humility, gentleness, patience, and bearing with one another. Being truly spiritual is not about how great our gifts are, but about how soft our hearts are. Humility overcomes pride, gentleness surpasses force, and patience dissolves conflict. When we lay ourselves down and let Jesus be King, unity grows naturally.

Paul then stresses the seven “ones”: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God. This is not an organizational slogan; it is spiritual reality. Our focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves, not on factions, not on backgrounds. When we return to this “one,” the unity of the Spirit is kept.

Finally, he says that everyone has been given a gift. No one is unnecessary, and no one can stand alone. Gifts are not for exalting ourselves but for building up the body. When each person offers themselves in selflessness, God’s divine order is built up.
Change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your daily living changes. When we shift from “Who am I?” to “Whose am I?”, we can live a life worthy of our calling.
a: Live out humility and gentleness today
In a situation that could turn into an argument, choose humility and patience.
Put your focus back on the “one Lord”
In any disagreement, ask yourself: Am I defending myself, or defending unity?
Discover and use the gift God has given me
Reflect: What gift has God measured out to me? How can I use it to bless others today?
q: Does the way I live match the calling God has given me?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for calling me to be Your child. Help me to live with humility, gentleness, and patience, and to keep the unity the Spirit gives. Let me not exalt myself, but lift up Jesus alone, so that my life is worthy of Your calling. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am called by God, and I live a life of humility and unity, letting Jesus be King within me.

t: Cry Out in the Wilderness, Be Brought Back by His Love
v: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever.
Let the redeemed by the LORD say so, whom he has redeemed from the hand of the adversary,
and gathered out of the lands, from the east and from the west, from the north and from the south.
They wandered in the wilderness in a desert way. They found no city to live in.
Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted in them.
Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses.
He led them also by a straight way, that they might go to a city to live in.
Let them praise the LORD for his loving kindness, for his wonderful deeds to the children of men!
For he satisfies the longing soul. He fills the hungry soul with good.
Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron,
because they rebelled against the words of God, and condemned the counsel of the Most High.
Therefore he brought down their heart with labor. They fell down, and there was no one to help.
Yet he lifts the needy out of their affliction, and increases their families like a flock.
The upright will see it, and be glad. All the wicked will shut their mouths.
Whoever is wise will pay attention to these things. They will consider the loving kindnesses of the LORD.
b: This psalm begins with a declaration: “He is good; his loving kindness endures forever.” This is not a slogan for easy times; it is a testimony from the wilderness. People wander, grow hungry and thirsty, lose heart, and even end up trapped in darkness because of rebellion. Yet at their most helpless moment, they “cried to the Lord,” and God delivered them.

The wilderness is not the end; it is the beginning of crying out. When people lay down their pride and admit they have lost their way, God leads them on a straight path. This is the turning point of a changed life: not how well I can find my way, but whether I am willing to cry out; not how capable I am, but whether I admit I need God.

The psalmist also honestly points out that some hardships come from human rebellion. When people go against God’s word, their hearts are weighed down by toil. Yet God’s discipline is not meant to destroy but to humble a hardened heart. His love is not indulgence; it is a bringing back.

In the end, God sets the needy on high and makes them flourish. The upright rejoice, and the wicked are silenced. The wise will pay attention to these things—not only looking at circumstances, but considering the loving kindness of the Lord.

True wisdom is not avoiding the wilderness, but learning to cry out in it; not denying failure, but seeing love in the midst of failure. When we turn from “holding it together by myself” to “crying out to God,” the wilderness becomes the road home.
a: Choose to cry out in hard times
When you feel lost, hungry, or empty, let your first response be prayer to God, not complaint.
Reflect on whether you have strayed
Honestly examine your path for any place where you have gone against God’s word, and be willing to repent and return.
Pay attention to God’s loving kindness
Write down one way God’s hand has guided you each day, and let your heart be filled with thanksgiving again.
q: Am I wandering in the wilderness right now, or have I learned to cry out to God in it?
pr: Heavenly Father, You are good, and Your loving kindness endures forever. When I am hungry and thirsty in the wilderness and my heart faints, teach me to cry out to You first. If I have wandered off on my own way, discipline me gently and bring me back to the right path. Lead me to the place You have prepared for me to live, and let me meditate on Your loving kindness all my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I cry out to the Lord in the wilderness, and he will lead me on the straight path by his loving kindness.

t: At the End of Life, What Remains Is Blessing
v: These are the days of the years of Abraham’s life which he lived: one hundred seventy-five years.
Abraham gave up his spirit, and died at a good old age, an old man, and full of years, and was gathered to his people.
Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron, the son of Zohar the Hittite, which is near Mamre,
the field which Abraham purchased from the children of Heth. Abraham was buried there with Sarah, his wife.
After the death of Abraham, God blessed Isaac, his son. Isaac lived by Beer Lahai Roi.
b: Abraham’s life can be summed up in one sentence: “an old man, and full of years, gathered to his people.” Scripture does not stress how much wealth he owned, but that he finished the task God entrusted to him.

A truly blessed person is not one who lived a spectacular life, but one who finished the course God gave him. From leaving Ur, Abraham learned along the way to trust God, obey God, and wait on God. He was weak at times and failed at times, but in the end he became the father of faith.

An even more moving picture is that his two sons, Isaac and Ishmael, together buried their father. Once separated by family conflict, they now stand together at their father’s grave. A life of faith can still bring reconciliation even after death.

That burial ground was the only piece of land Abraham truly owned in his lifetime. It was no grand palace, but a plot of faith. Before the promise was fully fulfilled, he chose to believe in God’s future. This is faith: preparing for eternity before seeing it.

The last line of the passage is even more striking: “After the death of Abraham, God blessed Isaac, his son.” A life that truly belongs to God does not stop when the body ends. Blessing continues, and grace is passed on.

This reminds us that the value of life is not in how much we receive, but in whether we leave blessing to the next generation. When a person lets God be King and wholeheartedly follows the Lord, his life becomes a flowing blessing.
a: Take stock of your life’s direction
Am I walking the road God called me to, or just chasing temporary achievements?
Value spiritual legacy
Is my life influencing the next generation so that blessing continues?
Prepare for eternity with faith
Lift your eyes from what you own on earth to God’s everlasting promises.
q: When my life is over, will what I leave behind be possessions, or blessing?
pr: Heavenly Father, teach me to live in Your promises like Abraham. Let me learn to trust in weakness and to obey while waiting. May my life not be lived for myself alone, but become a blessing that flows to the next generation. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I walk in God’s promises all my life, and let blessing continue from me to the next generation.

t: Parting Is Not the End; We Will Meet Again
v: But we don’t want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who have fallen asleep, so that you don’t grieve like the rest, who have no hope.
For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus.
For this we tell you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will in no way precede those who have fallen asleep.
For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel and with God’s trumpet. The dead in Christ will rise first,
then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. So we will be with the Lord forever.
Therefore comfort one another with these words.
b: These words were written to a church in the midst of pain. Someone had died, and hearts were full of longing and loss. Paul did not deny their sorrow; he only reminded them of one thing: our grief must not be like that of those who have no hope.

For those who believe in Jesus, death means something entirely different. Death is not disappearing; it is “falling asleep.” It is not an end, but a waiting. For the Lord we believe in has died and risen again. Since he is risen, those who are in him will rise too.

The most stunning line here is: “The Lord himself will descend from heaven.” He does not send an angel in his place; he comes himself. The Lord who gave his life for us will not leave his own alone in the grave. When the trumpet sounds, the dead in Christ will rise first, and we will meet the Lord together.

The climax of the whole passage is not the scene of being caught up, but the final line: “So we will be with the Lord forever.” The greatest blessing of heaven is not streets of gold, but being with the Lord forever.

So Paul says: comfort one another with these words. What faith gives us is not only peace in this life, but assurance for eternity. While we live, we live for the Lord; when we die, we are with the Lord; and when the Lord returns, we will meet him fully.
This hope means that even in the most painful parting of life, there is still light.
a: See death through the eyes of eternity
Look not only at what is lost now, but at the reunion to come.
Support one another in grief
Encourage one another with God’s promises instead of letting despair swallow the heart.
Live in the assurance of being with the Lord
Practice walking with the Lord today, for one day we will be with him forever.
q: When facing loss and parting, do I still live in the hope of resurrection and reunion?
pr: Lord Jesus, thank You for dying for me and rising for me. When I face parting and longing, comfort my heart with the hope of resurrection. Keep me from living in despair, and let me live in the assurance of eternity. May I walk with You in this life, and be with You forever in the life to come. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: In Christ I have the hope of resurrection, and one day I will be with the Lord forever.

t: Come Back, I Am Still Waiting for You
v: The LORD said to me, “Backsliding Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah.

Go, and proclaim these words toward the north, and say, ‘Return, you backsliding Israel,’ says the LORD; ‘I will not look in anger on you, for I am merciful,’ says the LORD. ‘I will not keep anger forever.

Only acknowledge your iniquity, that you have transgressed against the LORD your God, and have scattered your ways to the strangers under every green tree, and you have not obeyed my voice,’” says the LORD.
“Return, backsliding children,” says the LORD, “for I am a husband to you. I will take one of you from a city, and two from a family, and I will bring you to Zion.
I will give you shepherds according to my heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.

It will come to pass, when you are multiplied and increased in the land in those days,” says the LORD, “they will no longer say, ‘the ark of the LORD’s covenant!’ It will not come to mind. They won’t remember it. They won’t miss it, nor will another be made.

At that time they will call Jerusalem ‘The LORD’s Throne;’ and all the nations will be gathered to it, to the LORD’s name, to Jerusalem. They will no longer walk after the stubbornness of their evil heart.
b: What is most striking in this passage is not the judgment, but the call. God saw his people turn away, become false, and worship idols, yet he did not announce a final verdict. Instead he said, “Return!” This line reveals God’s nature: “I am merciful; I will not keep anger forever.” His anger is not revenge but discipline born of love; his heart is always waiting for them to turn back.

God shows that there is only one way back: “Only acknowledge your iniquity.” True repentance is not religious performance; it is admitting that we have gone our own way and made ourselves king. The heart of the problem is not the outward idols but the “stubbornness of their evil heart.” When people are willing to lay down their pride, return to their rightful place, and let God be God, life can be rebuilt.

Even more precious is God’s promise. He says, “I am a husband to you.” This is covenant language, a love that is never withdrawn. He will personally bring his people back to Zion and give them shepherds after his own heart, so that worship is centered on him again. Revival is not restoring forms; it is God sitting once more on his throne. When authority returns to God, his people no longer follow their own hearts, but live under his rule.
a: Face your own wandering honestly, and stop defending yourself.
Believe that God’s love is greater than your failures.
Let God be King again, and stop following a stubborn heart.
q: Do I hear God saying to me, “Return”?
pr: Merciful Father, thank You for calling me even when I went my own way. Give me a humble heart that confesses, so that I no longer follow my stubbornness but let You be King in my life. Bring me back into Your presence, to live in Your love. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I turn back to the Lord and let him be King in my life, living in his love that never leaves or forsakes me.

t: Fan Your Gift into Flame, and Let the Gospel Shine in You
v: For this cause, I remind you that you should stir up the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands.
For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.
Therefore don’t be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner; but endure hardship for the Good News according to the power of God,
who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before times eternal,
but has now been revealed by the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who abolished death, and brought life and immortality to light through the Good News.
For this I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a teacher of the Gentiles.
For this cause I also suffer these things. Yet I am not ashamed, for I know him whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to guard that which I have committed to him against that day.
Hold the pattern of sound words which you have heard from me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
That good thing which was committed to you, guard through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.
b: Paul wrote to Timothy from prison, not to make him shrink back, but to remind him: “Fan your gift into flame again.” A fire without fuel grows dim; faith that rests only on past inspiration also grows cold. God has already placed gifts within us, but we must work with the Holy Spirit to let them burn afresh. This fire is not of the flesh; it comes from God’s calling and grace.

What God has given us is not a spirit of fear. Fear comes from looking at circumstances, at ourselves, at difficulties; power, love, and self-control come from fixing our eyes on Jesus. Power keeps us from retreating, love keeps us from becoming cold, and self-control keeps us from losing control. Mature spiritual life is not impulsive passion, but a steady life with strength, love, and discipline.

Paul says, “I know whom I have believed.” The heart of faith is not how much I have done, but whom I know. Christ has abolished death and brought imperishable life to light. When we let the Holy Spirit dwell in our hearts as Lord, we can guard the good thing entrusted to us and not be shaken by the world. A flame lasts because its foundation is in the eternal Lord.
a: Check whether the fire within you is dimming, and return to prayer and truth.
When facing difficulty, don’t let fear lead; let strength and love lead the way.
Rely on the Holy Spirit to guard the mission God has entrusted to you, and don’t drift with the crowd.
q: Is my life cooling down, or being set on fire again by the Holy Spirit?
pr: Lord, thank You for placing gifts within me. Fan me into flame again with the Holy Spirit, so that I am no longer fearful but strong, loving, and self-controlled. Help me not to be ashamed of the gospel in any circumstance, and let my life shine for You until that day. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: By the Holy Spirit I fan my gift into flame, no longer fearful, and let the gospel keep burning in my life.

t: Still Choosing to Worship in the Ashes
v: So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD, and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head.
He took for himself a potsherd to scrape himself with, and he sat among the ashes.
Then his wife said to him, “Do you still maintain your integrity? Renounce God, and die.”
But he said to her, “You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. What? Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” In all this Job didn’t sin with his lips.

Now when Job’s three friends heard of all this evil that had come on him, they each came from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite; and they made an appointment together to come to sympathize with him and to comfort him.
When they lifted up their eyes from a distance, and didn’t recognize him, they raised their voices, and wept; and they each tore his robe, and sprinkled dust on their heads toward the sky.
So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.
b: Job lost his possessions, his children, and now even his body was struck, covered with sores from the sole of his foot to the top of his head. He sat in the ashes with only a broken piece of pottery in his hand. This is life at its lowest point. But what hurt even more than his body was his wife’s words: “Renounce God!” When even the closest person wavers, the test of faith runs deeper.

Job’s answer is shattering: “Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” He does not deny the pain; he still acknowledges God’s sovereignty within it. Mature faith is not only saying “Thank the Lord” in good times, but not sinning with our lips in hard times. When a person holds on to integrity in the ashes, God’s glory shines all the more truly.

His three friends came and sat beside him for seven days and seven nights without speaking. This passage reminds us that true comfort is not rushing to explain suffering, but being present. When someone is in great pain, a silent presence can sometimes be more powerful than a thousand words. God also often sits quietly with us in our most silent nights.
a: Guard your mouth in the valley
Don’t let bitterness replace worship; even through tears, don’t give up trusting.
Acknowledge God’s sovereignty
Learn to believe that God reigns, in blessing and in hardship alike.
Become a quiet companion
When others suffer, let your presence be better than empty comfort.
q: When I am in the ashes, does my mouth still choose to believe?
pr: Lord, in pain I do not understand, keep my lips from sinning. Help me still choose to trust You in the ashes, and still acknowledge that You reign even in brokenness. Teach me also to sit quietly with those who suffer, and to live out Your love. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Whether in blessing or in hardship, I still trust the Lord, and hold fast my integrity in the ashes.

t: He Isn’t Delaying; He Is Waiting for You to Turn Back
v: But don’t forget this one thing, beloved, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance.

But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night, in which the heavens will pass away with a great noise, and the elements will be dissolved with fervent heat; and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up.
Therefore, since all these things will be destroyed like this, what kind of people ought you to be in holy living and godliness,
looking for and earnestly desiring the coming of the day of God, which will cause the burning heavens to be dissolved, and the elements will melt with fervent heat?
But, according to his promise, we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.
Therefore, beloved, seeing that you look for these things, be diligent to be found in peace, without defect and blameless in his sight.
b: Many people ask, “Why hasn’t the Lord come yet?” Peter reminds us not to measure God’s work by human time. With the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. He is not delaying; he is waiting. Waiting for what? For people to repent. God’s silence is not indifference; it is the patience of love.

But the day of the Lord will surely come, suddenly, like a thief. Heaven and earth will dissolve, the glory of this world will pass away, and money, status, and reputation cannot last. Since this is so, what kind of people ought we to be? The answer is not panic but holiness and godliness. The focus is not on the details of the end times but on today’s life.

We are not waiting for destruction; we look for new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness dwells. Hope is not escaping reality but living out the values of the Kingdom. Since we will see the Lord, we should be diligent, so that we may stand before him at peace and without fear. True preparation is not guessing the time, but letting Jesus be King every day.
a: See today with eternal eyes
Don’t run only after short-term gain; learn to live in God’s time.
Treat repentance as grace
God gives me today as one more chance to turn back.
Live a prepared life
Be holy in small things and godly in daily life, and wait for the Lord in peace.
q: If the Lord came today, would my life be anxious, or at peace?
pr: Lord, thank You for not giving up on me, but waiting patiently for me to turn back. Help me not to waste the time You give, and to respond to Your love with holiness and godliness. Let me live in hope, preparing myself to meet You in peace. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I live in eternal hope, and every day I prepare to meet the Lord in peace.

t: Not Hiding in the Light, but Becoming the Light
v: “You are the salt of the earth, but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will it be salted? It is then good for nothing, but to be cast out and trodden under the feet of men.
“You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.
Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.
Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.
b: Jesus did not say, “Try hard to become salt and light.” He said, “You are.” This is a declaration of identity. When we are born again in Christ, the very nature of our life has changed. Salt exists to preserve and to season; light exists to drive out darkness and illuminate. Christians exist not to hide, but to influence.

If salt loses its flavor, it loses its use. When we are assimilated by the world and diluted by selfish desires, faith becomes only slogans and our lives have no power. If light is covered, it cannot shine. When we shrink back out of fear, compromise, or self-centeredness, the glory of God’s Kingdom is hidden. The focus is not on showing ourselves off, but on letting Jesus live out through us.

The Lord says the purpose of good works is not to glorify ourselves, but to cause people to glorify the Father. This is the order of life: first be connected to God, then shine in the world. Not holding it together by ourselves, but being led by the Holy Spirit; not exalting people, but exalting the Lord. When we live in selflessness, the light shines naturally.
a: Keep your flavor in daily life
At work, at home, and in relationships, live out Christ with honesty and gentleness.
Don’t let your light be covered
Stand boldly for truth, and don’t compromise because of circumstances.
Give the glory to God
Behind every good deed, acknowledge that it is God’s grace.
q: Does my life truly let people see light, or do they only hear slogans?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for giving me a new identity in Christ, making me the salt and light of the world. Guard my heart so that I am not diluted by the world or covered by fear. Let me live out Your glory every day, so that people see the good I do and give glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: In Christ I am salt and light, and I let the life of Jesus shine through me to the world.

t: When the Heart Is Set Ablaze, the Hands Begin to Give
v: All the congregation of the children of Israel departed from the presence of Moses.

They came, everyone whose heart stirred him up, and everyone whom his spirit made willing, and brought the LORD’s offering for the work of the Tent of Meeting, and for all of its service, and for the holy garments.

They came, both men and women, as many as were willing-hearted, and brought brooches, earrings, signet rings, and armlets, all jewels of gold; even every man who offered an offering of gold to the LORD.
Everyone with whom was found blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen, goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red, and sea cow hides, brought them.
Everyone who offered an offering of silver and bronze brought the LORD’s offering; and everyone with whom was found acacia wood for any work of the service, brought it.
All the women who were wise-hearted spun with their hands, and brought that which they had spun: the blue, the purple, the scarlet, and the fine linen.
All the women whose heart stirred them up in wisdom spun the goats’ hair.
The rulers brought the onyx stones and the stones to be set for the ephod and for the breastplate;
with the spice and the oil for the light, for the anointing oil, and for the sweet incense.
The children of Israel brought a free will offering to the LORD; every man and woman whose heart made them willing to bring for all the work, which the LORD had commanded to be made by Moses.
b: What is most moving in this passage is not the gold or the jewels, but the words “whose heart stirred him up” and “willing-hearted.” God was going to build the tabernacle, and he did not force anyone or assign quotas; he stirred hearts. When a heart is touched by God, giving is no longer pressure but joy.

Some brought gold, some brought cloth, some spun thread, some brought spices. Not everyone did the same thing, yet all had one purpose: to give God’s presence a dwelling place. This is a picture of God’s divine order: different gifts and different resources, yet working together in unity to accomplish God’s work. It is not about comparing who gave more, but about how each responded.

The key to giving is never the amount but the heart. When people truly experience salvation and their hearts are set ablaze by grace, they give naturally. If the heart is cold, no amount of appeals will help; if the heart is on fire, people have already prepared before the Lord even asks. What God values is not the outward worth, but the inner willingness.
a: Check whether your heart is still stirred
Toward the things of God, am I cold and watching from the sidelines, or is my heart moved?
Join the building with your gifts
Don’t compare with others; simply be faithful to offer what God has given you.
Let giving become joy
Entrust your time, ability, and resources to God, and count it an honor to walk with the Lord.
q: Is my offering right now out of pressure, or out of a willingness stirred by God?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for first showing me grace and touching my heart. Set the fire within me ablaze, so that I do not merely hear the call but willingly respond. Let me use all that You have given to take part in building Your Kingdom, and may the glory be Yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: My heart is stirred by God, and I willingly offer myself to take part in building his glorious work.
